questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Cervarix vaccine is effective against which of the following Human papillomavirus serotypes?
questions.explanation: The Cervarix vaccine is a bivalent vaccine specifically designed to protect against Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 16 and 18. These two high-risk serotypes are responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancers worldwide. HPV 6 and 11 (Option B) are low-risk serotypes that cause approximately 90% of genital warts; protection against these is provided by the quadrivalent (Gardasil) or nonavalent vaccines, but not by Cervarix. Options C and D list incorrect pairings of high and low-risk serotypes. Cervarix is typically administered to girls and young women before the onset of sexual activity to provide maximum preventative efficacy against cervical malignancy and its precursors. The vaccine works by inducing high levels of neutralizing antibodies against the L1 capsid protein of the virus. Universal HPV vaccination remains a primary public health goal for eliminating cervical cancer in many countries
questions.learning: The Cervarix vaccine is a bivalent vaccine specifically designed to protect against Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 16 and 18. These two high-risk serotypes are responsible for approximately 70% of all cervical cancers worldwide.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea, and laboratory testing shows elevated serum prolactin levels. MRI of the brain reveals a pituitary adenoma. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with hyperprolactinemia due to a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH, leading to the clinical triad of amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility. The first-line medical treatment for prolactinomas is dopamine agonists, such as Bromocriptine or Cabergoline. These medications effectively inhibit prolactin secretion and can lead to significant tumor shrinkage. Bromocriptine is particularly favored in women desiring pregnancy due to its established safety profile. Letrozole (Option B) is an aromatase inhibitor used for breast cancer and ovulation induction. Tamoxifen (Option C) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator used in breast cancer management. Goserelin (Option D) is a GnRH agonist used for endometriosis and prostate cancer. Surgical resection is only considered if medical therapy fails or if there are severe compressive symptoms like vision loss. Therefore, dopamine agonist therapy remains the primary intervention
questions.learning: The patient presents with hyperprolactinemia due to a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH, leading to the clinical triad of amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and infertility.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions do you see punched-out lesions of the retina?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis characteristically causes punched-out lesions in the retina.

Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infestation due to Toxoplasma gondii. It primarily affects the central nervous system and retina. In humans, it occurs as congenital, acquired, or recurrent.

Congenital toxoplasmosis is acquired by the transplacental route. Infants are usually born with inactive disease. Bilateral healed punched-out chorioretinal lesions in the macular area are usually seen. In acquired toxoplasmosis, punched-out lesions similar to congenital toxoplasmosis are seen. In addition, punctate outer retinal toxoplasmosis (PORT) may also be seen.

Other options:

Option A - Posterior staphyloma is used to describe a bulge in the sclera with the choroid behind the equator. On ophthalmoscopy, there is an excavated area with retinal vessels dipping in it.

Option B - Fundal coloboma occurs due to a defect in the closure of the embryonic cleft. It appears as a comet-shaped defect with the apex towards the disc which may or may not be involved. A few choroidal or retinal vessels may also be seen on the surface.

Option C - Congenital rubella typically produces a salt and pepper appearance of the fundus.
questions.learning: Toxoplasmosis Toxoplasmosis characteristically causes punched-out lesions in the retina. Toxoplasmosis is a parasitic infestation due to Toxoplasma gondii.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which physiological process operates through a mechanism similar to that of cervical dilation and fetal expulsion during uterine contractions?
questions.explanation: Cervical dilation and uterine contractions during labor are governed by a positive feedback loop known as the Ferguson reflex. As the fetal head stretches the cervix, more oxytocin is released, which in turn causes stronger contractions and further stretching. The physiological process that shares this exact positive feedback mechanism is milk ejection by oxytocin (Option A). Suckling at the breast sends signals to the brain that trigger oxytocin release; the resulting milk ejection encourages the baby to continue suckling, which further stimulates oxytocin release until the breast is emptied. Water retention by ADH (Option B) is a negative feedback loop designed to restore homeostasis. FSH secretion (Option C) is also primarily controlled by negative feedback from estrogen/inhibin. Therefore, the two core "oxytocin-driven" reproductive processes represent the classic examples of positive feedback in human physiology
questions.learning: Cervical dilation and uterine contractions during labor are governed by a positive feedback loop known as the Ferguson reflex. As the fetal head stretches the cervix, more oxytocin is released, which in turn causes stronger contractions and further stretching.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient presents with a recently developed fixed false belief in which a close family member, though identical in appearance, is perceived as an imposter. This delusion is causing marked distress and disruption in family interactions. This phenomenon is characteristic of a specific neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in certain forms of cognitive decline. In which type of dementia is this belief—where a familiar person is thought to be replaced by a look- alike—most commonly encountered?
questions.explanation: The belief that a familiar person has been replaced by a look-alike imposter is a specific delusion known as Capgras syndrome (or Capgras delusion). While it can occur in several psychiatric and neurological disorders, it is most commonly observed and highly characteristic of Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB). DLB is defined by its core features: fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations, and spontaneous motor features of parkinsonism. Capgras syndrome is thought to result from a disconnection between the brain's facial recognition system and its emotional appraisal system. Frontotemporal dementia (Option B) primarily presents with personality changes or language deficits. Vascular dementia (Option D) follows a "step-wise" decline related to cerebrovascular events. Embolism (Option A) is a cause of stroke but not a type of dementia. Recognizing Capgras syndrome in an elderly patient with cognitive decline is a vital clinical clue for differentiating DLB from Alzheimer's disease. Management involves the cautious use of atypical antipsychotics or cholinesterase inhibitors

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The O2 saturation with respect to PO2 is shown by the curve marked as 5. What happens to the oxygen Hb dissociation curve on transfusion of stored RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2

When stored RBCs are transfused, the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve typically shifts to the left but still retains its sigmoid shape as represented by the curve marked as 2.

This is due to reduced levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) in stored red blood cells. 2,3-BPG is a metabolite in RBCs that binds to hemoglobin and reduces its affinity for oxygen.

During storage, metabolic processes in RBCs slow down, leading to a depletion of 2,3-BPG. Lower 2,3-BPG levels make hemoglobin hold onto oxygen more tightly, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. Hence, this increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, shifting the curve to the left.

Other Options:

Option B and C: show a right shift to the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.↑ in 2,3-BPG seen in increased anaerobic glycolysis leads to the right shift of the curve. Storage of blood causes depletion of 2,3-BPG, hence leading to left shift instead of right.
questions.learning: 2 When stored RBCs are transfused, the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve typically shifts to the left but still retains its sigmoid shape as represented by the curve marked as 2.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with vaginal bleeding. What is the most likely diagnosis based on the image provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenomyosis

Adenomyosis is characterized on MRI by thickening of the junctional zone (>12 mm) with a heterogeneous “salt and pepper” appearance due to ectopic endometrial tissue and small cystic foci within the myometrium.

Signature Imaging Features:

• Thickened junctional zone (>12 mm)
• Heterogeneous myometrium
• Small myometrial cysts (T2 bright)
• Globular enlarged uterus

Endometrial tissue invades myometrium

↓

Repeated bleeding inside muscle

↓

Inflammation + fibrosis

↓

Junctional zone thickening

↓

Adenomyosis appearance on MRI

| Feature | Adenomyosis | Fibroid

| ------- | ----------- | -------

| Borders | Ill-defined | Well-defined

| Pattern | Diffuse | Focal

| MRI | Junctional zone thickening | Mass lesion

| Cysts | Present | Absent

MRI showing multiple intramural fibroids in the uterus
questions.learning: Adenomyosis Adenomyosis is characterized on MRI by thickening of the junctional zone (>12 mm) with a heterogeneous “salt and pepper” appearance due to ectopic endometrial tissue and small cystic foci within the myometrium.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Warthin Finkeldey cells are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rubeola

Warthin-Finkeldey cells are multinucleated giant cells that are present in the prodromal stage of measles (rubeola), HIV lymphadenitis, and various benign and malignant lymphoid conditions.

The cytopathic effect of measles consists of multinucleate syncytium formation with numerous acidophilic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions.

The image given below shows the Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells:

Measles is an infection caused by Paramyxovirus which is a single-stranded enveloped RNA virus. It spreads 4 days before and 5 days after the appearance of the rash through body secretions.

Clinical features include mild fever, conjunctivitis, upper respiratory tract infection, and pathognomic Koplik spots. The Koplik spots are red lesions with bluish-white spots seen in the inner cheeks at the level of premolars. The red maculopapular rashes begin on the forehead, behind the ears, and on the upper neck on the 4th day. It then spreads towards the torso, and extremities and reaches the palms and soles.

The diagnosis is mainly made clinically but a serological demonstration of IgM antibodies and IgG antibodies is also used. Complications include pneumonia, croup, and tracheitis. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a fatal complication of chronic measles diagnosed by elevated IgG levels in cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.learning: Rubeola Warthin-Finkeldey cells are multinucleated giant cells that are present in the prodromal stage of measles (rubeola), HIV lymphadenitis, and various benign and malignant lymphoid conditions.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of cartilage shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Elastic cartilage

The above image shows an elastic cartilage.

The elastic cartilage, like the hyaline cartilage, contains individual or small groups of chondrocytes that are surrounded by type II collagen fibrils. However, it differs from hyaline cartilage in that, much of the interterritorial matrix consists of fine yellow elastic fibres containing elastin protein.

On microscopy, elastic cartilage consists of:

• Chondrocytes within lacunae
• Elastic fibres in the matrix
• Perichondrium with outer fibrous layer and the inner cellular layer

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the most likely causative agent for a Tzanck smear showing multinucleated cells?
questions.explanation: A positive Tzanck smear is identified by the presence of multinucleated giant epithelial cells. This finding is classically associated with the herpesvirus family, most commonly Herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Varicella-zoster virus (VZV). While both can produce these giant cells, HSV is the most frequent clinical cause for localized herpetic lesions tested with this method. Human papillomavirus (Option C) causes warts and is characterized by koilocytosis rather than giant cells on Tzanck. Coxsackievirus A16 (Option D) causes Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease but does not result in a positive Tzanck smear. Therefore, when presented with this specific microscopic finding in a general diagnostic context, HSV remains the most likely causative agent for the observed multinucleation
questions.learning: A positive Tzanck smear is identified by the presence of multinucleated giant epithelial cells. This finding is classically associated with the herpesvirus family, most commonly Herpes simplex virus (HSV) or Varicella-zoster virus (VZV).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-month-old child undergoes treatment for diarrhoea with hypokalemia but the child does not respond to the treatment appropriately and on examination muscular weakness is noted, What is the most likely cause of treatment failure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypomagnesemia

The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia.

The major cause of hypomagnesemia in this scenario is severe diarrhoea/gastrointestinal loss which in turn worsens the hypokalemia. In such cases, hypokalemia can not be corrected unless the underlying hypomagnesemia is addressed.

Treatment failure in hypokalemia due to hypomagnesemia is mediated by two mechanisms:

* ↓ Magnesium → inhibits Na+/ K+ - ATPase activity → ↓ influx of potassium into the cell → secondary kaliuresis.

* ↓ Magnesium → decreased block of ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel) potassium efflux channels → increased potassium secretion by distal nephron

Therefore in the presence of hypomagnesemia, hypokalemic patients are clinically refractory to potassium supplementation therapy.

Hypokalemia is defined as a plasma concentration of K+ <3.5 meq/L. The following are various causes of hypokalemia:

* Inadequate intake

* Diet, potassium-free intravenous fluids, potassium deficient TPN

* Excessive potassium excretion

* Hyperaldosteronism

* Medications

* Potassium losses

* Direct loss of potassium from GI fluid (diarrhea)

* Renal loss of potassium (to conserve sodium in response to gastric losses)

* Metabolic

* Intracellular potassium shifts from metabolic alkalosis or insulin therapy

Clinical features

* Weakness and paralysis

* Intestinal ileus

* Risk of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias

* Broad flat T waves, ST depression, and QT prolongation are most marked when serum K+ <2.7 mmol/L

* Sodium chloride and bicarbonate retention lead to metabolic alkalosis

Management includes potassium supplementation with concurrent cardiac monitoring. Treat hypomagnesemia by supplementation. High dose propranolol if due to excess sympathetic activity

Other options:

Option B: The clinical features of hyponatremia are predominantly neurological as a result of the development of cerebral edema. Patients usually present with nausea, headache, vomiting, seizure, brainstem herniation, and coma.

Option C: The clinical features of hypermagnesemia are dose-dependent.

* >2 mmol/L - vasodilation and neuromuscular blockade.

* >4 mmol/L - refractory hypotension, progressive weakness leading to respiratory paralysis and coma. Although hypermagnesemia causes muscle weakness, the question asked is the cause of treatment failure in hypokalemia.

* >10mmol/L - dilated pupils, bradycardia, PR, QRS, and QT prolongation.

Option D: The clinical features of hypernatremia are neurological. The most frequent manifestation is altered mental status ranging from confusion and lethargy to deep coma.
questions.learning: Hypomagnesemia — The given clinical scenario of a child with diarrhea, muscular weakness, and hypokalemia not responding to treatment is most likely due to hypomagnesemia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A pregnant woman from a rural area registers under Janani Suraksha Yojana. Which of the following services would not be provided to her under this scheme?
options: Safe motherhood services under Vandematharam scheme
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. STD counseling

The Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) does not provide STD counseling.

Janani Suraksha Yojana is a safe motherhood intervention launched under National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional delivery among poor pregnant women. The services provided by the JSY are:

* Cash is disbursed to the mother at the institution for having an institutional delivery.

* Safe motherhood services (IFA tablets, Tt vaccination) under the Vandemataram scheme.

* Village health and nutrition day

* Maternal death review

* Pregnancy tracking: ASHA worker/Anganwadi Worker (AWW) or any other link worker help in monitoring antenatal check-ups, and post-delivery care.

* Safe abortion services: mifepristone followed by misoprostol and manual vacuum aspiration.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following diseases is unlikely to present with skin lesions on the shin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism is unlikely to present with skin lesions on shin. Myxedema (severe hypothyroidism) and pretibial myxedema are different entities. Pretibial myxedema is the infiltrative dermopathy (mucin deposition) seen over shin in Grave's disease, a type of hyperthyroidism.

Other options :

Option B: Diabetes: Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is classically seen on the anterior leg.

Option A: Sarcoidosis: Erythema nodosum may be seen on the anterior leg.
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism Hypothyroidism is unlikely to present with skin lesions on shin. Myxedema (severe hypothyroidism) and pretibial myxedema are different entities.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following is contraindicated in patients with acute intermittent porphyria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thiopentone

Thiopentone cannot be administered in a patient with acute intermittent porphyria.

Thiopentone is a barbiturate induces aminolevulinic acid synthetase, which increases the formation of porphyrins. This will precipitate porphyria attacks, especially acute intermittent porphyria or variegate porphyria in susceptible individuals.

Other effects:

Thiopentone

* is cerebroprotective as it reduces CSF volume by facilitating its absorption.

* also decreases cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume and helps in lowering intracranial pressure.

* should be avoided in hypovolemic or shock patients because of the significant reduction in cardiac output (69%) and arterial blood pressure due to vasodilation and venous pooling.

* produces dose-related central respiratory depression, producing a characteristic ventilatory pattern called 'double apnea'.
questions.learning: Thiopentone Thiopentone cannot be administered in a patient with acute intermittent porphyria. Thiopentone is a barbiturate induces aminolevulinic acid synthetase, which increases the formation of porphyrins.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old male patient with a history of cholecystectomy 4 years back for gallstones presents with symptoms of obstructive jaundice. Imaging studies reveal a stone in the common bile duct. What is the most probable type of stone causing this obstruction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary

| Type | Definition

| ---- | ----------

| Primary | Formed de novo within the bile duct itself

| Secondary | Migrated from the gallbladder into the CBD

| Retained | Missed at the time of cholecystectomy (found within 2 years of surgery)

| Recurrent | Found after 2 years of a previous stone-clear CBD

Why "Primary" is Correct Here

The key detail is the 4-year gap after cholecystectomy:

• The gallbladder has been removed → stone cannot have migrated from GB → rules out Secondary
• Discovered 4 years post-op → beyond the 2-year window → rules out Retained
• Stone formed de novo in the CBD after cholecystectomy = Primary stone

Characteristics of Primary CBD Stones

• Typically brown pigment stones (vs. cholesterol in secondary)
• Associated with bile stasis, infection (E. coli, biliary stricture)
• Often soft, earthy, and friable
• Seen with biliary stricture, periampullary diverticulum, or biliary dyskinesia
• E. coli produces β-glucuronidase → deconjugates bilirubin → pigment stone formation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: How can one measure an enzyme's catalytic activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vmax/[sₜ]

A homogeneous enzyme's catalytic activity is best described by its catalytic constant, kcat (Vmax divided by the number of active sites, sₜ).

kcat = Vmax/[sₜ]

While an enzyme's maximum capacity to convert substrate to product is important, the benefits of a high kcat can only be realised when Km is low enough. Thus, the catalytic efficiency of enzymes is best expressed as the ratio of these two kinetic constants, kcat/Km.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy presents with fever, weight loss, and a painless swelling in the jaw region. His CBC shows anemia with lymphocytosis, and biopsy of the swelling suggests a malignant process. Based on these clinical and laboratory findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a rapidly growing, painless jaw swelling in a child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt's lymphoma. The diagnostic histological hallmark, as seen in the provided image, is the "starry sky appearance". This pattern is created by large, pale-staining tingible-body macrophages (the "stars") that have phagocytosed apoptotic debris, scattered against a dense background of dark, rapidly dividing malignant B-cells (the "sky"). Hodgkin’s disease (Option A) would show Reed-Sternberg cells. Acute Lymphocytic Leukemia (Option B) usually presents with more generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly rather than an isolated jaw mass. Chloroma (Option C) is an extramedullary mass of leukemic cells associated with AML. Burkitt's lymphoma is associated with the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and a characteristic translocation involving the MYC gene. It is one of the fastest-growing human tumors but is often highly responsive to intensive chemotherapy
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a rapidly growing, painless jaw swelling in a child is highly characteristic of the endemic (African) form of Burkitt's lymphoma.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A three-year-old child presents with cough, wheeze, and recurrent infection for which he has been taking oral medications. He now presents with excessive weight gain, a round face, hirsutism, and hair growth in the forehead. Developmental milestones were normal, child's BMI is more than +2 standard deviation, but height for age is below -2 standard deviation. What is the next best step in management?
options: Checking for congenital hypothyroidism with T3, T4, TSH.
Checking for early morning cortisol and history of exogenous cortisol administration.
Advise exercise and dietary changes for the child.
Evaluate for genetic causes of obesity.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Checking for early morning cortisol and history of exogenous cortisol administration.

Exogenous Cushing syndrome should be suspected in a child with excessive weight gain, growth failure (short stature), and cushingoid features such as moon face, hirsutism, and facial fullness, especially with a history of recurrent respiratory illness suggesting possible prolonged corticosteroid use.

• Weight gain with decreased height velocity is a red flag for endocrine pathology (not simple obesity)
• Features like moon face, hirsutism, and truncal obesity point toward hypercortisolism
• Most common cause in children is exogenous steroid use (e.g., repeated oral steroids for wheeze/asthma)
• Initial step is to take a detailed drug history and check early morning cortisol (suppressed in exogenous cause)

Contrast:

• Simple obesity: weight gain with normal or increased height
• Hypothyroidism: weight gain is mild with lethargy, constipation, and delayed milestones
• Genetic obesity: usually early onset with normal or increased height initially

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the context of cervical cancer screening protocols, co-testing refers to performing which of the following diagnostic tests together?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HPV testing + Pap smear

Cervical Cancer is strongly associated with persistent infection by high-risk HPV types.

The most common oncogenic types:

• HPV 16
• HPV 18

Co-testing means performing: HPV DNA Test + Pap Smear

• Together in the same screening visit.
• Purpose:

| Test | Detects

| ---- | -------

| Pap smear | Abnormal cervical cells

| HPV DNA test | High-risk HPV infection

Screening Recommendations

| Age group | Recommended test

| --------- | ----------------

| 21–29 years | Pap smear every 3 years

| 30–65 years | Co-testing (HPV + Pap) every 5 years

| Alternative | Pap smear every 3 years

Persistent infection with high-risk HPV causes:

HPV infection

↓

Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN)

↓

Carcinoma in situ

↓

Cervical cancer

Thus detecting HPV early improves screening accuracy.

B) VIA + Pap smear

Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid

Used in low-resource settings, not standard co-testing.

C) Antibody testing + Pap smear

Antibody testing does not detect cervical precancer.

D) HPV testing + VIA

Not a standard screening combination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Human infection occurs through ingestion of quadrinucleate cysts in contaminated food or water. Which organism is most likely responsible for this infection?
questions.explanation: The ingestion of mature, quadrinucleate cysts via the feco-oral route is the standard mode of transmission for Entamoeba histolytica, the protozoan responsible for amoebiasis. Once ingested, these resistant cysts undergo excystation in the small intestine to release trophozoites, which can cause characteristic flask-shaped ulcers in the colon or extra-intestinal complications like liver abscesses. Giardia lamblia (A) also forms cysts, but these are typically ellipsoidal and contain four nuclei alongside distinct internal structures like axostyles. Cryptosporidium parvum (C) produces oocysts that are immediately infectious upon excretion but are not described as quadrinucleate in the same diagnostic context. Cyclospora cayetanensis (D) involves the ingestion of sporulated oocysts containing two sporocysts, each with two sporozoites. Because the term "quadrinucleate cyst" is the classic, high-yield descriptive hallmark for the infectious stage of E. histolytica in medical parasitology, it is the most accurate answer for this clinical vignette
questions.learning: The ingestion of mature, quadrinucleate cysts via the feco-oral route is the standard mode of transmission for Entamoeba histolytica, the protozoan responsible for amoebiasis.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain following alcohol consumption. Based on the provided X-ray, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a crescent-shaped pocket of air under the right dome of the diaphragm, which is the pathognomonic finding for Pneumoperitoneum (air in the abdominal cavity). In a patient with severe abdominal pain, this finding indicates a perforated hollow viscus, such as a perforated peptic ulcer or a ruptured bowel segment. SBO (Small Bowel Obstruction, Option B) would show multiple dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels. Esophageal perforation (Option C) and pneumomediastinum (Option D) typically present with air around the heart or in the neck tissues, rather than specifically under the diaphragm. Severe pain following alcohol intake could point toward a perforated gastric or duodenal ulcer. Pneumoperitoneum is a surgical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent laparotomy to find and repair the site of perforation. Erect abdominal and chest X-rays are the standard first-line investigations for identifying this critical sign
questions.learning: The X-ray displays a crescent-shaped pocket of air under the right dome of the diaphragm, which is the pathognomonic finding for Pneumoperitoneum (air in the abdominal cavity).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy presented with a white pupillary reflex for which enucleation was done. The histopathological examination of the specimen revealed Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. What could be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinoblastoma

This child with a whitish pupillary reflex and Flexner-Winterstein rosettes on histopathological examination has retinoblastoma. Flexner Winterstein rosettes refer to an arrangement of columnar cells around a central lumen, which is highly characteristic of retinoblastoma.

Retinoblastoma is a malignant proliferation of immature retinal neural cells and is the most common intraocular malignancy in children. It is associated with mutations in the RB1 gene at chromosome 13q14. It belongs to small round blue cell tumours because the immature retinal neural cells are seen as small round cells with large nuclei.

White pupillary reflex or leukocoria is the most common presenting feature, followed by a squint which is usually convergent. Rarely, the child may present with nystagmus and defective vision. Image below showing leukocoria of left eye

Histopathology of the tumor shows small round cells with large nuclei. Microscopic features of a well-differentiated tumour include Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (highly specific of retinoblastoma), Homer-Wright rosettes, pseudorosettes, and fleurettes formation. Areas of necrosis and calcification can also be seen.

The histopathological image of retinoblastoma is shown below.

Treatment typically involves chemotherapy plus focal therapy. The commonly used three-drug regimen is the CVE regimen consisting of Vincristine, Carboplatin, and Etoposide. Focal therapy includes cryotherapy, laser photocoagulation, thermotherapy, plaque radiotherapy, and external beam radiotherapy.

Enucleation is done when

* The tumor involves more than half of the retina

* The optic nerve is involved

* Glaucoma is present and the anterior chamber is involved

Other options:

Option B - Medulloblastoma is a malignant embryonal tumor of childhood that occurs exclusively in the cerebellum. Patients usually present with headaches, ataxia, and signs of brainstem involvement.

Histologically, the tumor is very densely cellular. Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and elongated or crescent-shaped hyperchromatic nuclei. Tumor cells form Homer Wright rosettes. They express neuronal markers such as synaptophysin.

Option C - Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood. The child usually presents with rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. There are 4 subtypes - embryonal, alveolar, botyroid, and pleomorphic. Cells show light microscopic features of striated muscle differentiation. Immunohistochemistry is positive for desmin.

Option D - Astrocytoma of the retina and optic nerve head is rare. It is usually asymptomatic and is most frequently seen in tuberous sclerosis. Fundus examination reveals a yellowish or white plaque, nodule, or mulberry-like lesion. These lesions are semitransparent peripherally and calcified centrally.

Image showing calcified astrocytoma:

Pearl PF1837: Histological Features of CNS Tumors

Pilocytic Astrocytomas:

* Biphasic architecture - loose microcystic component and dense fibrillary areas

* Bipolar cells (tumor cells): thin, long hairlike processes that are GFAP - positive.

* Rosenthal fibers: eosinophilic corkscrew - shaped inclusions

* Eosinophilic granular bodies: mulberry - like inclusions

Medulloblastoma:

* Very densely cellular, with sheets of small primitive appearing small blue cells

* Individual tumor cells have scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei that are frequently elongated or crescent-shaped

* Tumor cells form Homer - Wright rosettes (pseudorosettes) with a central neuropil

Ependymoma:

* Ependymal rosettes: gland - like round or elongated structures that resemble the embryologic ependymal canal, with long, delicate processes extending into the lumen

* Perivascular pseudorosettes: perivascular nuclear - free zone consisting of thin ependymal processes radiating toward the central blood vessel

Oligodendroglioma:

* Fried - egg appearance: sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm.

* Chicken - wire capillaries: a delicate network of anastomosing capillaries

Retinoblastoma:

* Composed of collections of small, round cells with hyperchromatic nuclei

* Flexner - Wintersteiner rosettes: arrangements of a single layer of tumor cells around an apparent lumen

* Homer - Wright rosettes: a ring of cells with an eosinophilic fibrillary center

* Fleurettes: retinoblastoma cells that have undergone greater photoreceptor differentiation and group together as a bouquet. Fleurettes lack mitosis or necrosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a 5-day history of fever and pain in the right lower abdomen. Examination reveals a tender mass in the right iliac fossa, and laboratory investigations show an elevated leukocyte count. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of acute right lower quadrant pain and fever progressing over several days, culminating in a palpable tender mass, is classic for an appendicular lump. This occurs when an acutely inflamed appendix is walled off by the greater omentum and adjacent loops of small bowel. The elevated leukocyte count confirms an active inflammatory/infectious process. Hydronephrosis (Option B) typically presents with flank pain radiating to the groin and would be felt in the lumbar region, not the iliac fossa. While intestinal tuberculosis (Option C) can present with an iliac fossa mass, it is usually more chronic and less acutely tender. Colon carcinoma (Option D) usually presents with a non-tender, hard mass and altered bowel habits in older patients. Management of an appendicular lump (the Ochsner-Sherren regimen) involves conservative treatment with antibiotics and observation, followed by interval appendectomy after 6–8 weeks, rather than immediate surgery, to avoid injury to the adherent bowel
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of acute right lower quadrant pain and fever progressing over several days, culminating in a palpable tender mass, is classic for an appendicular lump.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the usual position of the Golgi apparatus in serous acinar cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Supranuclear

Golgi complex is located in supranuclear cytoplasm in serous acinar cells. Serous acinar cells are generally found in pancreas and the submandibular salivary glands.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For which of the following conditions, surgery is indicated in a case of Fibroid Uterus? I. Symptomatic and failed medical management II. Size >12 weeks III. Pedunculated fibroid Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are the most common benign tumors of the uterus, arising from the smooth muscle cells of the myometrium. Surgery is indicated when fibroids cause significant symptoms, complications, or suspicion of malignancy, or when conservative treatment has failed.

All the listed conditions are indications for surgery:

• I. Symptomatic and failed medical management: Surgery is indicated in women with persistent heavy menstrual bleeding, pain, pressure symptoms, infertility, or recurrent pregnancy loss despite adequate medical therapy.
• II. Size >12 weeks: A uterus enlarged to more than 12 weeks’ gestational size is generally considered an indication for surgery, particularly if associated with rapid growth, pressure symptoms, or diagnostic uncertainty.
• III. Pedunculated fibroid: Pedunculated submucosal or subserosal fibroids are prone to torsion, degeneration, or prolapse, making surgical removal appropriate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding an allosteric modifier?
options: Causes the enzyme to work faster only.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Participates in feedback regulation

An allosteric modifier of an enzyme usually participates in feedback regulation.

Allosteric regulations are a natural example of control loops, such as feedback from downstream products or feedforward from upstream substrates. Allosteric regulation is also particularly important in the cell's ability to adjust enzyme activity.

An allosteric modifier or effector binds to the allosteric site to induce a conformational change in the catalytic or active site. Those modifiers or effectors that enhance the protein's activity are referred to as allosteric activators, whereas those that decrease the protein's activity are called allosteric inhibitors.

questions.text: Which of the following fibres reach the Purkinje cell directly?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Inferior olivary nucleus

The fibres of inferior olivary nucleus (climbing fibres) reach the purkinje cell directly.

Note:

The input from the Purkinje cells to the deep nuclei is inhibitory.

However, the deep nuclei output is always excitatory.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Efferent arteriolar constriction causes all except:
options: Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries
Increases hydrostatic pressure in glomerular capillaries
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries

Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries.

Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity of resistance.

Moderate efferent arteriolar constriction causes increased glomerular hydrostatic pressure and slightly increased GFR.

However, in cases of severe efferent arteriolar constriction (more than threefold increase in efferent arteriolar resistance), the renal blood flow is significantly reduced. This results in increased plasma protein concentration, thereby increasing the glomerular colloid oncotic pressure. As the increase in colloid oncotic pressure exceeds the increase in hydrostatic pressure, the net force for filtration decreases, resulting in decreased GFR.
questions.learning: Decreases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries Efferent arteriolar constriction increases oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries. Efferent arteriolar constriction has a biphasic response on GFR depending on the severity of resistance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient underwent an unsupervised delivery before reaching the hospital. Following delivery, she developed abdominal pain, breathlessness, hypotension, and tachycardia, with shock disproportionate to the amount of bleeding. On examination, a large mass is seen at the introitus, as shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterine inversion

The clinical scenario, along with the image showing a large mass at the introitus with no visible cervical os following an unsupervised delivery, is most consistent with uterine inversion.

Uterine inversion is a rare cause of postpartum collapse, which is acute in onset and occurs immediately after delivery.

Causes:

* Mismanagement of the 3rd stage of labor - Delivering a yet to be separated placenta (Crede’s method)

* Spontaneous

* Placenta accreta.

Features: Shock appears immediately after delivery and is disproportionately severe compared to the amount of bleeding, with features of both neurogenic and hemorrhagic shock. On abdominal examination, the uterine fundus is not palpable.

Management: The following steps are done in uterine inversion.

* Discontinue uterotonics

* Administration of IV crystalloids

* Repositioning is tried after confirming that the inverted uterus is not firmly retracted or contracted.

* Tocolytics such as terbutaline, magnesium sulphate, or nitroglycerin may be administered to relax the uterus and facilitate repositioning if the initial attempt fails.

* Oxytocin infusion is started, and tocolytics are stopped after repositioning. Await spontaneous expulsion of the placenta.

* The position of the uterus is maintained while applying bimanual compression.

* Surgical intervention is needed if repositioning fails or can't be done.

Vaginal operations

Abdominal operations

Hydrostatic method

Kustner

Huntington

O'Sullivan

Spinelli

Haultain

Oguchi

Other options:

Option A: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) or consumptive coagulopathy is a clinicopathologic condition marked by widespread fibrin formation within blood vessels, triggered by excessive protease activity in the blood that overwhelms the body’s normal anticoagulant defenses.

Option B: Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH): blood loss more than 500mL following birth of the baby (WHO). PPH is defined as the excessive bleeding following delivery (>500 mL in vaginal delivery or >1000 mL in cesarean delivery) accompanied by signs and symptoms of hypovolemia (ACOG-2017). In PPH, there is no history of mass seen at the introitus.

Option D: Uterine prolapse: The prolapsed portion visible at the introitus will show the opening of the cervical os.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to the outpatient department with fatigue, bone pain, and swollen, bleeding gums. On examination, petechiae are noted on the skin. Which treatment option is appropriate for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of swollen, bleeding gums, bone pain (due to subperiosteal hemorrhage), and petechiae on the skin is the classic presentation of Scurvy, caused by a profound deficiency of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid). Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen synthesis; its deficiency leads to weak connective tissues and fragile capillary walls. Vitamin A (Option A) deficiency causes night blindness. Vitamin D (Option B) deficiency causes rickets, which involves bone changes but not bleeding gums. Vitamin E (Option C) deficiency is rare and primarily neurological. Scurvy is often seen in children with highly restricted diets or neurodevelopmental disorders. Treatment involves oral Vitamin C supplementation, which leads to a rapid resolution of the bleeding and bone pain within days. Pediatricians must perform a detailed dietary history in children presenting with unexplained bruising or musculoskeletal pain to rule out this entirely preventable nutritional disorder
questions.learning: The clinical triad of swollen, bleeding gums, bone pain (due to subperiosteal hemorrhage), and petechiae on the skin is the classic presentation of Scurvy, caused by a profound deficiency of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy fell from the bed and developed swelling in the nose and difficulty in breathing. Examination revealed smooth rounded swellings on either side of the septum, through both the nares. On palpation, it was soft and fluctuant. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Incision and drainage

This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of a septal hematoma. The most appropriate next step in management would be incision and drainage of the hematoma.

Septal hematoma is caused due to collection of blood in between the perichondrium or periosteum and the cartilage of the nasal septum. It may be caused due to trauma, septal surgery, or spontaneously as in bleeding disorders.

Clinically, patients may present with bilateral nasal obstruction, pain, pressure over the nasal bridge, or a frontal headache. On examination, bilateral hematomas will be seen as purplish or reddish smooth swelling on either side of the septum. Palpation will reveal a soft, fluctuant swelling.

All septal hematomas must be drained to prevent the formation of septal abscess or organization of the hematoma by fibrosis leading to a permanently thickened septum. Drainage of the hematoma should be done either through aspiration with a wide gauge needle or through an incision made over the mucosa at the point of greatest fluctuation. It must be followed by nasal packing. Patients should thereafter be started on systemic antibiotics.

Given below are a clinical image and a illustrated image of septal hematoma.

Pearl PF1620: Septal Haematoma

* Septal hematoma is a collection of blood under the perichondrium or periosteum of the nasal septum

* Causes: Trauma, septal surgery and bleeding disorders

* Clinical features: Bilateral nasal obstruction (most common presenting feature), frontal headache

* Treatment:

* Aspiration of small hematomas

* Incision and drainage of large hematomas followed by nasal packing

* Systemic antibiotics to prevent abscess formation

* Complications: Septal abscess, depression of dorsum, permanently thickened septum
questions.learning: Incision and drainage — This clinical vignette is strongly suggestive of a septal hematoma. The most appropriate next step in management would be incision and drainage of the hematoma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with a chronic alcoholic patient presenting with gum bleeding, corkscrew hair, petechial haemorrhages, poor wound healing, and generalized weakness?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin C

The given clinical scenario of a chronic alcoholic patient presenting with gum bleeding, corkscrew hair, petechial haemorrhages, poor wound healing, and generalised weakness is associated with vitamin C deficiency.

Scurvy is a disease caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency, leading to impaired collagen synthesis and weakened connective tissue. It commonly occurs in individuals with poor dietary intake, such as chronic alcoholics, elderly individuals, and those with malnutrition.

Clinical features include gum bleeding, corkscrew hair, petechial haemorrhages, poor wound healing, generalized weakness due to fragile blood vessels and defective tissue repair. Other symptoms may include anaemia, joint pain, and swelling.

The cutaneous manifestations of scurvy include :

* Phrynoderma over posterolateral arms which can then generalize over the back and thighs and legs.

* Corkscrew hairs -  fractured and coiled hairs due to impaired keratin cross‐links by disulfide bonds

* Perifollicular hemorrhage and purpura

* Lower limb edema

* Splinter hemorrhages

Costo-chondral separation leads to the formation of tender nodules, which are sharply angulated, also known as the scorbutic rosary, as shown below.

Other radiographic features of scurvy include:

The white line of Frankel: calcified cartilage at metaphyses
Trumerfeld zone - a lucent zone beneath the Frankel's line due to lack of mineralization of osteoid
Pelkan spurs- due to fractures at the cortical margin
Periosteal elevation- due to subperiosteal hemorrhages

Scurvy is treated with vitamin C supplements of 100-200 mg/day orally or parenterally. The clinical improvement is seen within 1 week. The treatment should be continued for up to 3 months for complete recovery

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin A is an essential fat-soluble vitamin that plays a role in epithelial cell barrier function and immunity. Its deficiency is associated with diarrheal disease, weight loss, and malnutrition.

Option B: Vitamin B6, also known as pyridoxine, is a water-soluble vitamin essential for brain development, immune function, and protein metabolism. It helps the body produce neurotransmitters, red blood cells, and energy from food.

Option D: Vitamin B3, or niacin, supports energy production by aiding the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. It also helps maintain healthy skin, nerves, and digestive function.

Radiological features of scurvy:

* Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 23-year-old female visited the clinician with a solitary thyroid nodule and was advised for thyroid function tests where TSH level is 27.3 mU/L, T3 is 1.24 ng/ml, and T4 is 4.87 microgram/ml. Which of the following manifestations is true regarding the condition?
questions.explanation: The patient’s laboratory results show a significantly elevated TSH (27.3 mU/L) with normal to low-normal T3 and T4 levels, which is characteristic of primary hypothyroidism. Weight gain is a classic manifestation of hypothyroidism due to a decreased basal metabolic rate. Other typical symptoms include cold intolerance, constipation, bradycardia, and dry skin. In contrast, heat intolerance (Option A), tachycardia (Option B), and diarrhea (Option C) are hallmark symptoms of hyperthyroidism, where metabolic processes are accelerated. The most common cause of primary hypothyroidism in developed regions is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, while iodine deficiency remains a major cause globally. Given the high TSH, the body is attempting to stimulate a failing thyroid gland. Weight gain, puffiness, and lethargy are the most consistent clinical findings in this metabolic state
questions.learning: The patient’s laboratory results show a significantly elevated TSH (27.3 mU/L) with normal to low-normal T3 and T4 levels, which is characteristic of primary hypothyroidism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A child, upon disturbing a bee hive, had several stings. After a few minutes, the child developed breathing difficulty and hypotension. What is the drug of choice for managing this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adrenaline

The child has respiratory difficulty and signs of vascular collapse which is suggestive of anaphylactic shock and the drug of choice is adrenaline.

Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity.

Immediate (Type I) Hypersensitivity

* These are also called allergic reactions or allergies.

* They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals

* IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors; reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators.

* The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents; prostaglandins and leukotrienes; as well as cytokines.

* The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation).

* The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

* It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase.

Image: Sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity

Adrenaline 0.5 mg 1/1000 by intramuscular route (IM) is the drug of choice for treatment of anaphylactic shock.In case the patient develops life threatening condition, adrenaline 0.25 mg IV is given

Note:

* As vasodilatation is the main pathological change early in anaphylaxis, this enables the subcutaneous or intramuscular absorption of adrenaline to be rapid and effective.

* Thus, when the disease is treated early and is progressing slowly, or venous access is difficult or the patient is unmonitored, intramuscular adrenaline has advantages in terms of safety and is usually effective.

* Later, when intravascular volume is depleted and shock occurs with a life threatening situation, or there is severe dyspnoea or airway compromise, the intravenous route is necessary to achieve optimal absorption.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Melanin is derived from which of the following amino acids?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tyrosine

Melanin is derived from tyrosine.

Products derived from tyrosine:

* Melanin

* Catecholamines e.g epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine

* Thyroxine

Tyrosine is a precursor of melanin, thyroxin, epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA).

* Formation of DOPA: Tyrosine is hydroxylated by tyrosinase to form dihydroxy phenylalanine or DOPA. Tyrosinase is a monooxygenase that contains copper.

* Formation of melanin: Tyrosinase acts on DOPA to form dopaquinone, which is then converted to indolequinone. The indolequinone is polymerized to form melanin.

* Formation of catecholamines: Epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine. They are produced by the adrenal medulla and sympathetic ganglia.

* Tyrosine is first hydroxylated to dihydroxyphenylalanine (DOPA) by tyrosine hydroxylase.

* DOPA is decarboxylated by DOPA decarboxylase to form dopamine.

* Dopamine is further hydroxylated to norepinephrine or noradrenaline

* Norepinephrine is then methylated by the enzyme N-methyl transferase (NMT) to form epinephrine or adrenaline. S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is the methyl donor.

The series of reactions involving the production of catecholamines is shown in the image below.

* Formation of thyroid hormones: Tyrosine residues are iodinated to form 3-mono-iodo-tyrosine (MIT) and 3,5-di-iodo-tyrosine (DIT). These are coupled to give rise to triiodothyronine (T3) and tetraiodothyronine (thyroxine or T4)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
The latent period, contraction period, and relaxation period of a skeletal muscle are 10 ms, 40 ms, and 50 ms respectively. Calculate the tetanizing frequency.

ms- millisecond
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 25 per second

The tetanizing frequency of the given skeletal muscle is 25 per second.

In the question, it is given that the contraction period is 40 msec (40 msec is 0.04 seconds)

Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period

Therefore, tetanizing frequency = 1/40 millisecond = 1/0.04 per second = 1000/40 per second = 25 per second.

When there is a repeated stimulus to a muscle fiber before relaxation, it produces an additional contraction of the muscle. The second contraction adds to the first contraction and the total strength of contraction increases. This phenomenon is known as a summation of contractions.

With repeated stimulation, contraction occurs repeatedly before any relaxation has occurred. This causes the individual responses to fuse into one continuous contraction. Such a response is called tetanus (tetanic contraction).

Tetanizing frequency is the minimum frequency required for producing tetanus.

Tetanus is of two types.

• Complete tetanus- when no relaxation occurs between stimuli
• Incomplete tetanus- when periods of incomplete relaxation occur between the summated stimuli.

* Palpated against the underlying tarsals

* It is palpated on the dorsum of the foot in the first intermetatarsal space just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Surgical excision is carried out, and microscopic examination of the tumor along with molecular studies reveals abnormalities in cell cycle regulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The 3-year-old boy presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and a missing red reflex, which are the hallmark clinical signs of retinoblastoma—the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. Disrupted cell cycle regulation (Option B) mentioned in the molecular analysis refers to the inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13, which is the underlying genetic cause. Wilms tumor (Option A) is a kidney malignancy. Ependymoma (Option C) is a CNS tumor. Neuroblastoma (Option D) is an extracranial solid tumor. Microscopic examination of retinoblastoma classically shows small blue round cells with characteristic Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Because the clinical findings are exclusively intraocular and the genetic profile matches RB1 dysfunction, retinoblastoma is the correct diagnosis. Early detection is vital for preserving vision and the life of the child through therapies like chemotherapy, cryotherapy, or enucleation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old female presenting with an unsteady gait, forgetfulness, labile moods, and Kayser-Fleischer rings was diagnosed with Wilson's disease. Which of the following options correctly indicate the gene mutated in this condition and its location?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ATP7B gene on chromosome 13

Wilson's disease, an autosomal-recessive disorder is caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13

The ATP7B gene, located on chromosome 13, encodes a transmembrane copper-transporting ATPase, expressed on the hepatocyte canalicular membrane. Deficiency in the ATP7B protein causes a decrease in copper excretion into the bile, impairs its incorporation into ceruloplasmin, and inhibits ceruloplasmin secretion into the blood, leading to the accumulation of toxic levels of copper in the liver, brain, and eye.

Note:

Menkes disease is an X-linked metabolic disturbance of copper metabolism caused by mutations in the copper-transporting ATP7A gene.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 22-year-old mother presented with her 3 week-old newborn who had a large tongue and a umbilical hernia. Which of the following investigations has to be done in view of congenital hypothyrodism?
options: A fresh blood sample and screen first for TSH levels
A fresh blood sample and screen first for T4 levels
A dried blood sample and screen first for TSH levels
A dried blood sample and screen first for T4 levels
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. A dried blood sample and screen first for TSH levels

The most commonly followed strategy for newborn screening of congenital hypothyroidism is using a dried blood sample and screening it first for TSH.

Screening for children for congenital hypothyroidism is very important, as early diagnosis and treatment can help in normal intellectual development. Otherwise, congenital hypothyroidism is known as the most common preventable cause of mental retardation. Children diagnosed beyond the neonatal period have a poor outcome.

Screening is usually done on day 2-day 4 postnatally, and programs usually use dried blood samples for this. The most commonly used strategy screens for TSH first as they have higher sensitivity compared to the T4-based approach. Although the TSH-based approach is better, it doesn't identify central hypothyroidism, which can be identified by the T4-first approach. But, the T4-based approach misses out on the cases of compensated hypothyroidism.

The incidence of congenital hypothyroidism seems to be 4 times higher in India compared to western countries. Thyroid dysgenesis has emerged as the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism in India accounting for about 75% of all cases. Interestingly, an Increased incidence of thyroid dysgenesis is noted in Down syndrome.

Management: Thyroid replacement soon after the diagnosis. Thyroxine of dose 10-15 μg/kg/day should be started and adjusted to achieve normal free T4 range. TSH may be elevated up to 2 years of age with reset of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

Superior border of infraorbital rim and inferior border of external auditory canal

Correct answer: A. Inferior border of infraorbital rim and superior border of external auditory canal

The Frankfurt horizontal plane is an important anthropometric reference plane used in ENT, dentistry, maxillofacial surgery, and radiology to standardize head position. It is a line joining:

• Inferior orbital margin (orbitale)
• Superior border of external auditory canal (porion)

This plane should be parallel to the ground when the head is in anatomical position.

• Standard head positioning in cephalometry
• Planning orthognathic and facial surgeries
• Radiographic skull measurements
• Anthropometric facial analysis

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The following diagram charts the population change over years from 1983 to 1989 in a given place. What is the statistical diagram used here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Component bar graph

The given image shows a component bar graph or a component bar chart. The bars can be divided into two or more parts where each part represents a certain item, proportional to the magnitude of that particular item (males and females in this image).

It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data.

The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups. Frequency polygon and Ogive can be constructed using a histogram, not a component bar chart

Pearl PF0302: Graphical Representation of Data

1. Histogram

* A histogram, by definition, is a graphical representation of frequency distribution that contains rectangles and shows the underlying frequency of a set of continuous, quantitative data.

* The X or horizontal axis is called the abscissa which usually has the group scores or class intervals of the variables/data and the Y or vertical axis is called the ordinate which usually shows the frequencies at which these variables appear.

* The following is a histogram of cholesterol levels from the Framingham Heart Study.

2. Bar Chart

* It is also called a bar graph.

* It is used mainly for nominal or ordinal scale data as they are not quantitative and usually qualitative.

* The difference between a bar graph and a histogram is that the rectangles are separated by spaces representing data that forms discrete categories instead of continuous groups.

* Bar graphs can be simple, multiple or component bar graphs.

3. Pie Charts

* Pie charts are also used for nominal or ordinal data.

* The categorical data are represented as segments of a circle.

4. Frequency polygons

* Frequency polygons are used for mainly ratio and interval scale data.

* In a frequency polygon, the mid-points of each class interval are joined together by straight lines.

5. Ogive

* A frequency polygon which is drawn to represent cumulative frequency distributions form a typical S-shaped curve which is called an ogive. It referred to as a cumulative frequency diagram.

6. Line chart

* It is also called a line diagram or line graph.

* Its best use is to show the trend of events or change over passage of time.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 38-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after suffering a stab injury to the lower chest. On presentation, he had bradycardia and hypotension which did not improve despite IV fluid administration. Chest radiography showed clear lung fields. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. eFAST

The given clinical scenario of a patient with a stab injury and hypotension not responding to IV fluids indicates persistent hypotension due to ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST.

Cardiogenic shock or hemorrhagic shock are the most likely causes of persistent hypotension in a trauma patient. Ultrasound evaluation using eFAST to look for pericardium, pleural cavities, and abdomen in combination with plain radiographs of the chest and pelvis will usually identify the source of the bleed.

In patients with persistent hypotension due to blunt trauma, the pelvis should be wrapped in a sheet for stabilization until radiography can be done.

Evaluation of CVP or ultrasound of the IVC may further assist in distinguishing between cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock.

It is mostly fatal if not controlled, and requires immediate management. Blood and plasma transfusions are provided in a ratio of 2:1. Patients with persistent hypotension requiring surgical intervention include:

• Blunt trauma and massive hemothorax
• Penetrating trauma
• Hemoperitoneum
• Gunshot injuries to the chest or abdomen
• Penetrating weapon remaining in place.

Other options:

Options C and D: CECT can be done only when the patient is hemodynamically stable.

Option B: Tube thoracostomy has no role in this patient's management since the X-ray shows clear lung fields.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are precipitating factors for hepatic encephalopathy? 1. Hypokalemia 2. Septicemia 3. Increased dietary protein load Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2 and 3

Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in patients with advanced liver disease or portosystemic shunting. It is most commonly precipitated by factors that increase ammonia production, decrease ammonia clearance, or worsen cerebral susceptibility to ammonia.

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. Hypokalemia: Correct. Hypokalemia increases renal ammonia production and promotes metabolic alkalosis, facilitating ammonia entry into the brain, thereby precipitating HE.
• Statement 2. Septicemia: Correct. Septicemia (infection) is a common precipitating factor due to increased catabolism and systemic inflammation.
• Statement 3. Increased dietary protein load: Correct. Increased dietary protein load (especially in susceptible patients) increases intestinal ammonia production and can precipitate HE.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 3 Hepatic encephalopathy (HE) is a potentially reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome seen in patients with advanced liver disease or portosystemic shunting.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A randomised control trial is being conducted in patients with direct inguinal hernia, to compare the outcomes of a new surgery 'A' and the gold standard surgery 'B'. The p value of this trial is found to be 0.04. What can we conclude from this?
options: Type II error is small and we can accept the findings of the study
The probability of false negative conclusion that operation A is better than B is 4%
The power of the study to detect the difference between operation A and B is 96%
The probability of a false positive conclusion that operation A is better than B is 4%
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. The probability of a false positive conclusion that operation A is better than B is 4%

Since the p-value of the study is found to be 0.04, we can infer that the probability of a false positive conclusion that the operation A is better than B is 4%.

In this scenario, the p value is 0.04 which makes it, by convention, statistically significant. We can reject the null hypothesis and accept the alternative hypothesis that operation A is better than operation B.
questions.learning: The probability of a false positive conclusion that operation A is better than B is 4% Since the p-value of the study is found to be 0.04, we can infer that the probability of a false positive conclusion that the operation A is better than B is 4%.

questions.text: Which is not seen in pregnancy induced hypertension:
options: Systemic hypertension within 10 weeks of gestation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Systemic hypertension within 10 weeks of gestation

Hypertension induced by pregnancy is gestational hypertension which is characterized by BP more than 140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks of gestation in a previously normotensive woman.

The incidence of gestational hypertension and preeclampsia is remarkably increased in diabetic mothers.

40% of pregnant women with diabetes will develop preeclampsia. Chronic hypertension with overt diabetes increased the risk of preeclampsia to 60%

Hypertension is a risk factor associated with the progression of diabetic retinopathy.

The platelet count is usually found to be decreased in gestational hypertension.

Correct answer: A. Chancroid

Multiple painful genital ulcers 3 days after unprotected intercourse is indicative of Chancroid or Soft Chancre.

Chancroid is a type of sexually transmitted infection (STI) that is caused by the bacterium Haemophilus ducreyi, a gram-negative coccobacillus. It presents with painful genital ulceration along with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy that may develop into buboes. Auto-inoculation by the organism can result in new ulcers merging with the older ones. Hence, they are called "kissing ulcers."

The diagnosis is made clinically and can be supported by the school of fish/railroad track appearance on Gram stain (bacilli arranged in small groups, or parallel chains) as shown below:

First-line management is azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose or ceftriaxone 250mg IM in a single dose.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the demographic cycle, which phase is characterized as the low stationary phase?
questions.explanation: The demographic cycle represents the stages of population change over time. Phase 1 is the "high stationary" stage (high birth and death rates). Phase 2 is "early expanding" (birth rates remain high, death rates fall). Phase 3 is "late expanding" (birth rates start to fall). Phase 4 is correctly identified as the "low stationary phase". In this stage, both birth rates and death rates have stabilized at a very low level, resulting in zero or very slow population growth. Many developed nations are currently in Phase 4. Phase 5 is "declining" (birth rates fall below death rates). Understanding these phases is vital for long-term health planning, as the transition from Phase 2/3 to Phase 4 usually correlates with increased urbanization and better access to family planning. A nation's economic and social development can often be predicted by its current position in this demographic cycle
questions.learning: The demographic cycle represents the stages of population change over time. Phase 1 is the "high stationary" stage (high birth and death rates).

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Whole Bowel Irrigation (WBI) as a method of gastrointestinal decontamination is useful for poisoning with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iron

Whole Bowel Irrigation (WBI) is a method of gastrointestinal decontamination in which large volumes of polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solution (PEG-ELS) are administered orally or via a nasogastric tube to rapidly flush the gastrointestinal tract. It is particularly useful for substances that are poorly adsorbed by activated charcoal, such as iron.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Alcohol ❌

• Alcohols are rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, so WBI is ineffective.

• C. Kerosene ❌

• Gastric decontamination is contraindicated due to the high risk of aspiration pneumonitis.

• D. Organophosphorus ❌

• Management focuses on airway support, atropine, and pralidoxime; WBI has no routine role.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 20-year-old pregnant female presents with conductive hearing loss of 54db, not associated with tinnitus. Pure tone audiometry shows a notch at 2000 Hz. Which of the following is correct regarding the pathophysiology of the disease?
options: Ossicular fixation with intact tympanic membrane
Ossicular fixation with perforated tympanic membrane
Erosion of stapes footplate with perforated tympanic membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ossicular fixation with intact tympanic membrane

The given clinical scenario of a young pregnant female with bilateral conducting hearing loss and notch at 2000Hz (Carhart's notch) is suggestive of otosclerosis where there is an ossicular fixation with the intact tympanic membrane.

Otosclerosis is the disease of the bony labyrinth in which a normally dense endochondral layer of the bony otic capsule is replaced by irregularly laid spongy bone. It has a positive family history with an autosomal dominant trait. It is more commonly seen in females between 20-30 years of age and the hearing loss is aggravated during pregnancy and menopause. It may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta and a viral infection like measles.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fissula ante fenestram. There is fixation of stapes footplate.

Patients present with a bilateral conductive type of hearing loss, tinnitus (commonly in cochlear type and active stage), paracusis willisii (better hearing in noisy surroundings than in a quiet place), vertigo, and a monotonous, well-modulated soft speech.

The tympanic membrane is quite normal and mobile. Eustachian tube function is also normal. Pure tone audiometry shows a dip at 2000 Hz in the bone conduction curve known as the Carhart's notch. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

On examination, Schwartz sign/flamingo flush showing a red blush of the tympanic membrane due to vascularity can be seen.

Treatment includes medical, surgical management, and hearing aids. Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage to speed up the maturity of the active focus and halt further cochlear loss. The treatment of choice is surgical management which includes stapedotomy/stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Hearing aids are used in patients who refuse or are unfit for the surgery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has lost sensation over the dorsum of the foot and medial 4 toes. There is associated difficulty of eversion of the foot. Which nerve injury is likely to be the reason for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superficial peroneal nerve

Loss of sensation/paresthesia/numbness in the dorsum of the foot along with loss of eversion of the foot is due to injury to the superficial peroneal nerve.

The peroneus longus (principle evertor of the foot) in the lateral compartmentof the leg, is innervated by the superficial peroneal nerve. Damage to the superficial peroneal nerve would result in loss of eversion at the sub-talar joint.

The lateral compartment of the leg is supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. It consists of peroneus longus and peroneus brevis.

Other options:

* Foot drop occurs due to common peroneal nerve injury and sensory loss would involve the front and outer half of the leg and the whole dorsum of the foot. A high stepping gait is seen in this nerve injury.

* The posterior tibial nerve will involve loss of sensation over the sole of the foot. This is also the nerve involved in tarsal tunnel syndrome.

* The deep peroneal nerve innervates all muscles of the anterior compartment which are the dorsiflexors of the foot, extensor digitorum brevis, first two dorsal interossei muscles, and skin between great and second toes.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 25-year old man presents with a history of urethral discharge for the last three days. A gram stain smear of the discharge is shown below. All of the following are true regarding the likely etiology except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obligate intracellular organism

The given slide shows gram-negative diplococci within the polymorphs, characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Neisseria is not an obligate intracellular organism, it can also occur extracellularly i.e, it is a facultative intracellular organism. The other neisseria that are found as normal inhabitants of the human respiratory tract occur extracellularly.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative, non-sporulating, non-motile diplococcus that is aerobic but may grow anaerobically also. It is oxidase and catalase-positive.

Although Neisseria are non-motile organisms, they show twitching motility. This is a flagella-independent form of bacterial translocation over moist surfaces that occurs by the extension and retraction of polar type IV pili. These pili act as virulence factors by promoting attachment to host cells and inhibiting phagocytosis.

Virulence factors for gonococci:

1. Outer Membrane Proteins (OMPs)
2. IgA proteases
3. Pili
4. Lipo-oligosaccharide (LOS)
