questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 20-year-old woman visits the OPD with complaints of irregular menses since menarche and increased facial hair. Her BMI is 29 kg/m2 and her Ferriman-Gallwey score was 6. Her testosterone level was 0.36 ng/dl. Her mother is a diabetic on oral hypoglycemic agents. She should be advised the following, except?
options: Counselled about risk of metabolic syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. OCPs + Anti-androgens

This patient's history of irregular menstrual cycles and increased facial hair and hirsutism as per the Ferriman-Gellway score are suggestive of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Anti-androgens are not recommended in the initial therapy of PCOS.

Hormonal therapy in PCOS is initiated with combined OCPs which are useful in treating menstrual abnormalities, reducing acne, and hirsutism. Anti-androgens arerecommended in PCOS only if patients have no improvement in hirsutism after 6 months of therapy with OCPs alone. Further, a serum testosterone level of 0.36 ng/dl is within the normal range (0.2-0.8 ng/dl) there is no current indication to begin anti-androgen therapy in this patient.

PCOS is an endocrinopathy seen in women of reproductive age, affecting multiple systems. Rotterdam criteria is used to diagnose PCOD. The presence of two of the three components of this criteria establishes the diagnosis:

• Oligo/amenorrhoea, anovulation, infertility
• Hirsutism/acne
• Ultrasound findings:

• Enlarged ovaries with ovarian volume will be more than 10 mm3
• 12 or more small follicles each of 2-9 mm in size placed peripherally

Ultrasound image given below shows an enlarged ovary seen in PCOS with multiple follicles in the periphery.

Patients with PCOS are at risk of developing metabolic syndrome (Syndrome X), characterised by abdominal obesity, high blood pressure, impaired fasting glucose, high triglyceride levels, and low HDL cholesterol levels.

Treatment of PCOD:

• Lifestyle changes (Option C) such as weight reduction, smoking cessation, are recommended and most important in preventing metabolic syndrome (Option D).
• Fourth-generation oral contraceptive pills (OCP) (Option A) containing ethinyl estradiol and drospirenone are used for treating menstrual abnormalities, reducing acne, and hirsutism.
• OCP with cyproterone acetate is prescribed for PCOS patients with hirsutism.
• Patients with PCOD are prone to developing insulin resistance, which can be controlled with metformin. Acarbose can be used as an alternative if metformin is contraindicated.
• Infertility in PCOD patients is treated with clomiphene as the first-line drug for inducing ovulation. Dexamethasone is used in combination to improve fertility rates. Letrozole is used off-label in clomiphene-resistant cases.

Surgical options include laparoscopic ovarian drilling or puncture of not more than four cysts in each ovary. This is done either by laser or by unipolar electrocautery. It restores endocrine levels and improves fertility. Surgery is indicated only if:

• Medical therapy fails
• Hyperstimulation occurs
• Infertile women
• Previous pregnancy losses
questions.learning: OCPs + Anti-androgens — This patient's history of irregular menstrual cycles and increased facial hair and hirsutism as per the Ferriman-Gellway score are suggestive of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: All of the following are features of SIRS except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Respiratory Rate > 20/minute and PaCO2 <35 mmHg

Respiratory Rate > 20/minute or (Not and) PaCO2 < 32 mmHg (Not <35 mmHg) would be a feature of SIRS (Systemic inflammatory response syndrome).

Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) is an exaggerated defense response of the body to a noxious stressor (infection, trauma, surgery, acute inflammation, ischemia, or reperfusion) to localize and then eliminate the endogenous or exogenous source of the insult.

SIRS is diagnosed when any two of the following are present:

• Hyperthermia (>38 Degree Celsius) or Hypothermia (<36 Degree Celsius)
• Tachypnoea (>20/min) or PaCO2 < 32 mmHg
• Tachycardia (>90/min)
• White cell count >12 x 109/liter or <4 x 109/liter or >10% Band forms

Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection.
questions.learning: Respiratory Rate > 20/minute and PaCO2 20/minute or (Not and) PaCO2 38 Degree Celsius) or Hypothermia ( 20/min) or PaCO2 90/min) • White cell count >12 x 109/liter or 10% Band forms Sepsis is SIRS with a documented infection.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions does not contraindicate the use of beta-blockers?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism does NOT contraindicate the use of beta-blockers. In fact, beta-blockers can be used safely and are sometimes even beneficial in hypothyroid patients. Hypothyroidism is associated with decreased heart rate and reduced cardiac output, and while beta-blockers further slow the heart, they are not absolutely contraindicated. Moreover, beta-blockers are classically used in hyperthyroidism to control sympathetic overactivity symptoms, but hypothyroidism itself poses no direct contraindication to their use. Why other options are wrong: (A) Asthma is incorrect because asthma is a absolute contraindication to beta-blockers, especially non-selective ones like propranolol. Beta-blockade causes bronchoconstriction by blocking β₂ receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, potentially triggering life-threatening bronchospasm in asthmatic patients. (B) Glaucoma is incorrect as a contraindication because beta-blockers like timolol eye drops are actually used TO TREAT glaucoma by reducing aqueous humor production. Therefore glaucoma is not a contraindication but rather an indication for beta-blockers. (C) Bradycardia is incorrect because bradycardia is a absolute contraindication to beta-blockers. Since beta-blockers slow AV conduction and reduce heart rate, administering them to an already bradycardic patient can cause severe bradycardia, heart block, or even cardiac arrest
questions.learning: Hypothyroidism does NOT contraindicate the use of beta-blockers. In fact, beta-blockers can be used safely and are sometimes even beneficial in hypothyroid patients.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best non-invasive tool for assessing fetal anaemia?
options: Middle cerebral artery doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Middle cerebral artery doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV)

Middle Cerebral Artery Doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV) is the best non-invasive way of monitoring fetal anemia.

MCA PSV is used for the monitoring of fetuses of Rh-negative sensitized mothers, and if it exceeds 1.5 MoM and the gestational age less than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling followed by transfusion is considered.

Serial measurements of the peak systolic velocity of the fetal MCA is reliable, noninvasive, and the recommended test to detect fetal anemia. Blood gets shunted to the brain to maintain adequate oxygenation. A rise in cardiac output and a fall in blood viscosity enhance the peak systolic velocity in the MCA.

The threshold value to identify fetuses with anemia is 1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) for gestational age and is 100% sensitive.

For an MCA PSV between 1.0 and 1.5 MoM, weekly Doppler monitoring to be done. If MCA PSV exceeds 1.5 MoM and the gestational age is lesser than 34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling followed by fetal transfusion to be done if needed.

Beyond 34 weeks, the false-positive rate of MCA peak systolic velocity increases due to the normal increase in cardiac output that develops at this gestational age.

Middle cerebral artery velocimetry is more accurate than and has replaced amnionic fluid spectral analysis and is not associated with the risks of increased alloimmunization and amniocentesis. It is also applied clinically to evaluate fetal growth restriction.

Other Options:

Option A: Biophysical profile, aka Modified Manning score, is a screening test for uteroplacental insufficiency. The fetal CNS is highly sensitive to diminished oxygenation and helps plan the next course of action.

Option B: If the MCA peak systolic velocity > 1.5 MoM and the gestational age is <34 or 35 weeks, fetal blood sampling should be considered and followed by fetal transfusion if needed. But it will fall under invasive method.

Option C: Amniocentesis is the most common prenatal diagnostic procedure. It is performed using an aseptic technique, under direct sonographic guidance, using a 20–22 gauge spinal needle.Approximately 20 to 30 mL of fluid is collected for fetal karyotyping or chromosomal microarray analysis.
questions.learning: Middle cerebral artery doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV) Middle Cerebral Artery Doppler peak systolic velocity (MCA PSV) is the best non-invasive way of monitoring fetal anemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are responsible for corneal transparency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratan sulfate

The glycosaminoglycan (GAG) responsible for corneal transparency is keratan sulfate.

Glycosaminoglycans or mucopolysaccharides are complex carbohydrates made up of amino sugars and uronic acids. They may be attached to a protein molecule to form a proteoglycan.

Keratan sulfate is a mucopolysaccharide that does not contain uronic acid. It is constituted by repeating disaccharide units of N-acetyl glucosamine and galactose.

Keratan sulfate is present between the collagen fibrils in the cornea and plays a major role in corneal transparency.

2 types of keratan sulfate are seen:

• Keratan sulfate I is present in the cornea.
• Keratan sulfate II is mainly present in the cartilage.

Keratin sulfate I and II differ in their linkage to the core proteins. Keratan sulfate I links to a core protein L-asparagine via N-acetylglucosamine and Keratan sulfate II to  L-Serine (or L-Threonine) via N-acetylgalactosamine.

The chemical structure of Keratan sulfate is shown in the image below.

Other options:

Option B: In chondroitin sulfates (chondroitin 4-Sulfate & chondroitin 6-Sulfate), the repeating disaccharide units are glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine.  They maintain the structure of the extracellular matrix (ECM) and are located in endochondral bone and cartilage. They are also found in the ECM of the central nervous system. They act as signaling molecules in the prevention of the repair of nerve endings after injury.

Option C: Heparan sulfate is found on many extracellular cell surfaces and contains glucosamine with fewer N-sulfates than heparin. The predominant uronic acid is d-glucuronic acid. In the plasma membrane of cells, they act as receptors and mediate cell growth and cell-cell communication. It is also found in the basement membrane of the kidney along with type IV collagen and laminin, where it determines the charge selectiveness of glomerular filtration.

Option D: Hyaluronic acid is present in synovial fluid. It is also found in skin, bone, cartilage, vitreous humor, and embryonic tissues. It contains repeating units of N Acetyl Glucosamine and glucuronic acid. It plays a role in morphogenesis and wound repair. The high concentrations of hyaluronic acid along with chondroitin sulfates in cartilage contribute to its compressibility.
questions.learning: Keratan sulfate — The glycosaminoglycan (GAG) responsible for corneal transparency is keratan sulfate. Glycosaminoglycans or mucopolysaccharides are complex carbohydrates made up of amino sugars and uronic acids.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with pregnancy-induced hypertension and requires pharmacological treatment. Which of the following drugs is considered safe for managing this condition during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Managing hypertension in pregnancy requires drugs that are effective for the mother while being non-teratogenic for the fetus. Alpha-methyldopa (Option C) is the gold-standard, first-line antihypertensive in this setting. It is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist with a long-established safety profile and no known adverse effects on fetal development. Lisinopril (Option A), an ACE inhibitor, and Losartan (Option D), an ARB, are strictly contraindicated throughout pregnancy as they are highly teratogenic, causing fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, and skull ossification defects. Propranolol (Option B) is generally avoided as it may be associated with intrauterine growth restriction and neonatal hypoglycemia. Labatalol and Nifedipine are other common alternatives, but among the choices provided, Alpha-methyldopa is the classic and definitive safe choice for pregnancy-induced hypertension management
questions.learning: Managing hypertension in pregnancy requires drugs that are effective for the mother while being non-teratogenic for the fetus. Alpha-methyldopa (Option C) is the gold-standard, first-line antihypertensive in this setting.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While calculating the infant mortality rate, what population is represented in the denominator?
questions.explanation: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is a critical indicator of a nation's overall health status and socio-economic development. It is defined as the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1,000 live births in a given year. Therefore, the numerical denominator used to express this rate is 1,000. Rates expressed per 100 (Option A) are simple percentages. A denominator of 100,000 (Option D) is used for the Maternal Mortality Ratio, reflecting the much rarer occurrence of maternal deaths. Option C (10,000) is not a standard multiplier for vital health statistics. IMR is influenced by various factors including maternal health, nutrition, and access to neonatal care. Reducing IMR is a primary goal of global health initiatives like the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG 3). Accurate reporting using the standard per-thousand denominator allows for the comparison of health performance across different regions and time periods, guiding policy decisions and resource allocation for pediatric care
questions.learning: The Infant Mortality Rate (IMR) is a critical indicator of a nation's overall health status and socio-economic development. It is defined as the number of deaths of infants under one year of age per 1,000 live births in a given year.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text:
A 6-year-old girl born out of nonconsanguineous marriage presented with rachitic changes in limbs since 1½ years of age for which she has received multiple courses of vitamin D. Investigations showed the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Parameter
Lab determined value

Calcium
9.5 mg/dl

Phosphate
1.6 mg/dl

Alkaline Phosphatase (ALP)
814 IU

Serum Parathyroid hormone (PTH)
Normal levels

Serum electrolytes
Within Normal Limits (WNL)

Serum creatinine
Within Normal Limits (WNL)

Arterial Blood Gas analysis (ABG)
Within Normal Limits (WNL)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypophosphatemic rickets

A history of resistant rickets with normal levels of calcium (9 to 11 mg/dL), parathyroid hormone (PTH), arterial blood gas (ABG), with decreased phosphate (normal - 2.5 to 4.3 mg/dL), and elevated levels of alkaline phosphatase (ALP) (normal, 33 to 96 U/L) in a child is suggestive of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Hypophosphatemic rickets:

X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) is the most common genetic cause of rickets while the most common, overall is nutritional vitamin D deficiency. Mutations in the PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase on x chromosome) leads to increased FGF-23 (phosphatonin), which inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule levels and hence, causes increased excretion of phosphate. It also inhibits renal 1-alpha hydroxylase leading to reduced 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D.

Causes of hypophosphatemic rickets include familial vitamin D resistance, autosomal dominant hypophosphatemic rickets, autosomal recessive hypophosphatemic rickets, tumor-induced rickets, McCune Albright syndrome, epidermal nevus syndrome, and neurofibromatosis.

In X-linked dominant hypophosphatemic rickets lower extremity abnormalities, short stature, poor growth, delayed dentition, and tooth abscesses are common.

The chart attached below summarizes the evaluation of hypophosphatemic rickets.

Patients with hypophosphatemic rickets respond well to oral phosphorus and 1,25-D (calcitriol). Phosphorus supplementation is usually given in 1-3 g elemental phosphorus divided into 4–5 doses. Frequent dosing reduces diarrhea, which is a complication of high-dose oral phosphorus.

Calcitriol is administered 30–70 ng/kg/day divided into 2 doses. Burosumab, a monoclonal antibody to FGF-23 can be used in children > 1 year of age with XLH rickets.

Further, Joulie's solution is also useful in the treatment of familial hypophosphatemic rickets. Joulie's solution includes contains 30.4 mg of phosphate/mL. The most common side effect is diarrhea.

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A is due to mutation in the gene coding for 1α-hydroxylase leading to reduced calcitriol levels (1,25-D). Type 1B is due to a mutation in the gene for 25-hydroxylase leading to reduced calcidiol (25-D). Type 2A have mutations in the gene coding for vitamin D receptor. Type 2B is due to the over-expression of a hormone response element-binding protein that interferes with the actions of 1,25-D. All of them have normal to low calcium levels, low phosphorus, elevated PTH and ALP levels.

Option B: Hypoparathyroidism will present with features of hypocalcemia. There will be a decrease in serum PTH levels and calcium levels.

Option C: In chronic renal failure, 1α-hydroxylase activity is reduced leading to reduced 1,25-D. They have normal to low calcium levels and elevated PTH and ALP levels. They have hyperphosphatemia due to decreased renal excretion of phosphate.

The image below summarizes the common features of rickets in children.

questions.text: Highest Sodium content is present in which of the following foods:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Canned soup

Highest Sodium content is present in Canned Soup.

Packaged, processed, store-bought, and restaurant foods have highest amount of sodium in the form of salt added as a preservative to the canned foods.

Other options: Sugar cane, Barley, Fresh fruit juices all have less sodium content when compared to canned soup.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Can you identify the active toxic compound found in the poisonous plant shown in the image below?
questions.explanation: The image shows Atropa belladonna (Deadly Nightshade), identifiable by its characteristic shiny black berries, bell-shaped purple flowers, and broad oval leaves. The active toxic compound found in this plant is 1-hyoscyamine (which racemizes to atropine upon extraction). Key Plant Identification Features visible in image : The plant shows classic Atropa belladonna features — glossy black round berries, drooping purple bell-shaped flowers, and broad green leaves growing alternately. All parts of the plant are toxic, especially the berries which are attractive to children. Mechanism of Toxicity : 1-Hyoscyamine is a tropane alkaloid that acts as a potent competitive antagonist at muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, producing classic anticholinergic toxidrome — dry mouth, mydriasis, flushing, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, and delirium ("mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, red as a beet"). Why other options are wrong: (A) Calotropis gigantea is incorrect because Calotropis contains calotropin and calactin (cardenolide glycosides). It appears as a shrub with thick fleshy leaves and purple crown-shaped flowers — entirely different morphology. (B) Digitalin is incorrect because digitalin is the toxic compound found in Digitalis purpurea (Foxglove), which has tall spikes of tubular pink/purple flowers — completely different appearance from the plant shown. (C) Ricin is incorrect because ricin is the toxic compound found in Ricinus communis (Castor bean plant), which has distinctive star-shaped leaves and spiny seed pods — morphologically very different from Atropa belladonna
questions.learning: The image shows Atropa belladonna (Deadly Nightshade), identifiable by its characteristic shiny black berries, bell-shaped purple flowers, and broad oval leaves.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 6-month-old child is brought to the OPD with a deformity as shown in the image given below. Which of the following is your line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Manipulation and cast

The first line of management of the given image, congenital vertical talus deformity (CTEV), is manipulation and cast by Ponseti's method.

Congenital Vertical Talus deformity/Rocker-Bottom foot: It is a rare deformity usually affecting both feet where the medial arch is not only flat, it is also the most prominent part of the sole, producing the appearance of a rocker-bottom foot. The talus points almost vertically towards the sole.

Management:

* The first line management for CTEV is Ponseti's technique in which gradual correction of deformities is done by plaster cast. The sequence of correction is given as:

*         C- Cavus

*         A- Adduction

*         V- Varus

*         E- Equinus

*         Ponseti's method is the currently used method for conservative management of CTEV.

* When passive correction is not possible. ‘Reverse Ponseti’ technique (where the foot is stretched into plantar-flexion and inversion while counter pressure is applied to the medial aspect of the head of the talus), 4-5 plaster casts are usually required until the plantar-flexed talus is in line. This is followed by stabilization of the talonavicular joint with an open approach.

Following is the image of congenital vertical talus which has pre-operative, intraoperative and postoperative radiological images.

Ponseti's method is currently used for the conservative management of congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), while Kite's method was previously followed. Conservative management is preferred for CTEV

Kite's method (Not used now)

<2 weeks of age

adduction - inversion -equinus

Below is the image of CTEV/Clubfoot.

Pearl PF1915: Age wise management of CTEV

Initial treatment starts with Ponseti's POP cast as early as possible, but within 1 year of age.

If deformity gets corrected:

* Dennis Brown splint is used till 1 year of age

* After 1 year upto 5 years CTEV shoes are used in day, and Dennis Brown splint is used at night

If deformity is not corrected or untreated previously:

* 1-3 years: Posteromedial soft tissue release (PMSTR)

* 3-5 years: Dillwyn Evans procedure

* 5-8 years: Dwyer osteotomy

* 8-10 years: Wedge tarsectomy

* >10 years: Triple arthrodesis, external fixators

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The cover-uncover test is performed to diagnose various eye conditions. Which of the following is not detected by this test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Amblyopia

The cover-uncover test cannot detect Amblyopia.

This test consists of two parts:

* Cover test

* Uncover test

Cover Test: This is used to detect heterotropia (Manifest Squint) (Option B). Light is first shone and corneal reflections are observed. This is done to assess fixation in the deviating eye. The procedure for testing using an accommodative target and for distance is as follows.

* The patient is asked to fixate on a target straight ahead.

* The eye in which deviation is not suspected is covered first. For example, if a right eye deviation is suspected, the left eye is covered.

* Any movement of the right eye to take up fixation is noted.

* The following are the possible results:

Movement of the eye
Suspected defect

No movements
Orthotropia/ Heterotropia of the covered eye

Adduction
Exotropia

Abduction
Esotropia

Downward movement
Hypertropia

Upward movement
Hypotropia

The test is then repeated for the opposite eye.

Uncover test: This is used to detect heterophoria (latent squint)(Option A). The test is performed for both near and distant as follows.

* The patient fixates a distant target straight ahead.

* The examiner covers an eye for 2-3 seconds and the cover is then removed.

* If the covered eye had deviated, a re-fixation movement is observed on being uncovered.

* The following are the possible results based on the re-fixation movements of the eye.

Movement of the eye
Suspected defect

No movements
Orthophoria

Adduction (Nasal recovery)
Exophoria

Abduction
Esophoria

Downward/Upward movement
Vertical phoria

* The speed and smoothness of the recovery is noted as well as evidence of the strength of motor fusion.

* The test is then repeated for the opposite eye.

Other options:

Option C: Amblyopia is a developmental defect of spatial visual processing that occurs in the central visual pathways of the eye.  Generally, a difference of two lines or more on an eye chart test of visual acuity between the two eyes or a best-corrected vision of 20/30 or worse would be defined as amblyopia.

Treatment modalities include:

* Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/ day) using patches. It allows an amblyopic eye to be used.

* Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine. Instilling atropine into the fixing eye, forces the squinting eye to be used for seeing near objects.

Pearl PF1402: Cover tests in ophthalmology

Cover–uncover test:

* To detect the presence of heterophoria: Latent squint

* One eye is covered with the occluder, and the other eye is made to fix an object.

* In the presence of heterophoria, the eye under the cover will deviate.

* When the cover is removed, the eye under the cover will return back to its normal.

* This movement is observed.

* The direction of movement determines the type of heterophoria.

Direct Cover test:

* Confirms the presence of manifest squint.

* Differentiates apparent squint from a manifest squint.

* The patient is asked to fixate on the point light.

* The normal-looking eye is covered.

* In manifest squint, the uncovered eye will move in the opposite direction to take fixation.

* In apparent squint, there will be no movement of the uncovered eye.

Alternate cover test:

* In the below image, the patient has right exotropia with left eye fixating.

* Both eyes move each time the cover alternates from one eye to the other.

* It reveals if the squint is unilateral or alternate.

* It differentiates between concomitant and paralytic squint.
questions.learning: Amblyopia — The cover-uncover test cannot detect Amblyopia. This test consists of two parts: * Cover test * Uncover test Cover Test: This is used to detect heterotropia (Manifest Squint) (Option B).

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient’s laboratory results were positive for malarial antigen, and the Widal test findings were as follows: O ag >1:300, H ag >1:20, A >1:20, B >1:20. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Widal test is used to detect antibodies against the somatic (O) and flagellar (H) antigens of Salmonella typhi and paratyphi. A significantly elevated titer of only the O antigen (>1:100 is typically considered significant in India) indicates a recent or active infection. In this case, the O antigen titer is markedly high (>1:300), while the H, A, and B titers are at baseline levels. A past infection (Option C) or the recovery phase (reconvalescence, Option D) would typically show elevated H titers as O antibodies disappear first. If the patient had received the TAB vaccine (Option B), one would expect to see an elevation in multiple flagellar antigens (H, AH, and BH). Therefore, the isolated and high O antigen titer confirms that the patient is currently in the acute stage of a Salmonella infection

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following primary second messengers is involved in the contraction of ciliary muscles while focusing on near objects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IP3

IP3 is the primary second messenger involved in the contraction of ciliary muscles to focus on a near object.

On focusing on a near object, stimulation of the parasympathetic nerve fibers leads to the contraction of the bilateral ciliary muscle, via short ciliary nerves, which relaxes the lens ligaments. The lens becomes thicker and the increase in the refractive index allows the eye to focus on the near object. This is known as the accommodation reflex.

In the ciliary muscles of the eye, contraction is mediated via M3 > M2 receptors, while relaxation is mediated via the β2 receptor.

M3 receptors act via the formation of inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG), leading to an increase in intracellular Ca2+ and activation of protein kinase C, respectively. The increase in intracellular Ca2+ sets up a chain reaction which eventually leads to contraction of the ciliary smooth muscle of the eye.

Thus, in the contraction of the ciliary muscle during focusing on a near object, the second messenger involved is the IP3-DAG pathway.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the approximate time interval between HIV infection & manifestation of AIDS?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 10 years

The time interval between primary HIV infection and the manifestation of AIDS is 10 years.

After exposure to the HIV virus, there occurs primary infection following an incubation period of 2-4 weeks, which is usually symptomatic in more than 50% of cases, following 3-6 weeks there is acute HIV syndrome due to wide dissemination of the virus, characterized by fever, sore throat, diarrhea, lymphadenopathy, and rash.

This peak viremia drops as the immune response develops, to reach a plateau about 3 months later. Following this there is a prolonged period of clinical latency, during which infected individuals are asymptomatic, lasting for a median of 10 years.

Following this period, chronic persistent infection develops which is the hallmark of HIV disease called Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS).

Long-term non-progressors: a small part of untreated HIV-infected people with CD4 counts within the reference range for >10 years.

Elite controllers: Some long-term non-progressors have undetectable viral loads.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the action of the muscle at the hip, which is attached to the marked area in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Extension and lateral rotation

The image shows the posterior surface of the femur, and the structure marked is gluteal tuberosity, to which the gluteus maximus muscle is attached. It causes extension and lateral rotation at the hip joint.

The femur can be divided into:

• The proximal femur - Consists of the head, neck, greater and lesser trochanters. The intertrochanteric line is present on the anterior surface at the junction of the neck and shaft of the femur while the intertrochanteric crest is present on the posterior surface.
• The shaft of the femur - Consists of linea aspera (bony crest present on the posterior surface), gluteal tuberosity, and pectineal line
• The distal femur - Consists of the medial condyle, lateral condyle, intercondylar fossa, and patellar surface

The image below shows attachments of various muscles over the posterior surface of the right femur.

Gluteus maximus muscle:

Origin:

• Posterior aspect of the dorsal ilium, posterior to the posterior gluteal line
• Posterior superior iliac spine
• Posterior aspect of sacrum and coccyx
• Sacrotuberous ligament.

Insertion - It is inserted mainly in fascia lata at the iliotibial band and also into the gluteal tuberosity on the posterior femoral surface.

Action:

• Major extensor of the hip joint
• Lateral rotation of the hip joint
• Active in powerful abduction of the thigh

Arterial Supply - Inferior and superior gluteal arteries and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery.

Nerve Supply- Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1 and S2).
questions.learning: Extension and lateral rotation — The image shows the posterior surface of the femur, and the structure marked is gluteal tuberosity, to which the gluteus maximus muscle is attached.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The image shows two data distribution curves from separate studies within the same population: one depicted with a red line and the other with a blue line. Given the graphical representation, which of the following correctly represents the relationship among the mean, median, and mode for the data presented?
options: Mean = median, not equal to mode
Mode = median, not equal to mean
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mean = median, not equal to mode

The curve shown represents a symmetrical distribution with an abnormal peak, where mean equals median, but mode differs. This pattern commonly occurs in bimodal or irregular symmetric distributions. Therefore, the correct relationship is mean = median ≠ mode.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In controlled tipping, the amount of land required for the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000 is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1 acre

In controlled tipping, one acre of land is required by the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000.

It is also known as a sanitary landfill. It is the most satisfactory method of refuse disposal where suitable land is available. In this method, waste material is placed in a trench or other prepared area. Then, it is adequately compacted and covered with earth at the end of the day.

Methods used in controlled tipping are:

• Trench method: Done in places where level ground is available
• Ramp method: Well suited where the terrain is moderately sloping
• Area method: Used for filling land depressions, disused quarries, and clay pits
questions.learning: 1 acre In controlled tipping, one acre of land is required by the trench method to be practiced for a population of 10,000. It is also known as a sanitary landfill.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with chronic cough and shortness of breath. Bronchoscopy reveals increased neutrophils and macrophages within the airways. Which of the following enzymes released by these inflammatory cells is primarily responsible for the tissue destruction seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elastase

Cigarette smoking recruits neutrophils and macrophages into the lungs, where they release elastase, a proteolytic enzyme that degrades alveolar elastic fibers. In smokers, oxidative stress also inactivates α₁-antitrypsin, the major inhibitor of elastase, resulting in unopposed elastase activity and progressive destruction of alveolar walls, leading to emphysema (COPD).

• AAT deficiency: Causes panacinar emphysema (predominantly lower lobes) and may be associated with liver disease.
• Smoking-related emphysema: Centrilobular (centriacinar) emphysema, predominantly affecting the upper lobes.

Why not the other options?

• A. Elastin: A structural protein of the extracellular matrix, not an enzyme.
• B. Peroxidase: Enzyme involved in microbial killing by neutrophils; it does not cause alveolar destruction.
• D. Collagenase: Degrades collagen and contributes to tissue remodeling, but elastase is the principal enzyme responsible for emphysematous destruction.
questions.learning: Elastase Cigarette smoking recruits neutrophils and macrophages into the lungs, where they release elastase, a proteolytic enzyme that degrades alveolar elastic fibers.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the heart chamber marked as shown in the CT image below?
questions.explanation: On an axial CT scan of the heart, the four chambers are organized in a predictable anatomical relationship. The chamber marked in the image is the most posterior chamber, which is situated directly anterior to the esophagus and the descending aorta. This is definitively the Left Atrium (Option D) . The Right Ventricle (Option B) is the most anterior chamber, located just behind the sternum. The Right Atrium (Option A) forms the right border of the heart. The Left Ventricle (Option C) forms the apex and the left lateral border. Because the arrow points to the base of the heart posteriorly, where the pulmonary veins enter, the left atrium is the only correct anatomical identification. This structural knowledge is essential for interpreting CT and MRI scans in patients with suspected valvular disease or atrial enlargement

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
Which of the following drugs is a β2 agonist?

1. Dopexamine

2. Dipivefrine

3. Fenoldopam

4. Mirabegron
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2

Dipivefrine and dopexamine are β2-adrenergic receptor agonists.

Dipivefrine causes a decrease in aqueous production and increases outflow. It was used in the treatment of open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension but has since been replaced.

Dopexamine is a synthetic analogue related to dopamine with activity at D1 and D2 receptors as well as at β2 receptors. It is used in patients with severe congestive heart failure, sepsis, and shock.

Other options:

B. Fenoldopam is a peripheral D1 agonist with moderate affinity for α2-adrenergic receptors. It is a rapidly acting vasodilator that is used in severe hypertension.

D. Mirabegron is a β3-adrenergic receptor agonist which is used for bladder incontinence. Activation of this receptor in the bladder leads to detrusor muscle relaxation and increased bladder capacity. This action prevents voiding and provides relief for those with an overactive bladder and urinary incontinence.
questions.learning: 1, 2 Dipivefrine and dopexamine are β2-adrenergic receptor agonists. Dipivefrine causes a decrease in aqueous production and increases outflow.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: All of the following ions have decreased concentration on the luminal side of proximal convoluted tubule except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Chloride

The concentration of chloride on the luminal side is more when compared to sodium, glucose, and amino acids.

In the first half of the proximal tubule, sodium is reabsorbed by co-transport along with glucose, amino acids, and other solutes. As sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, it preferentially carries glucose, amino acids, bicarbonate along with it. Thus, their concentrations decrease markedly along the length of the proximal tubule, and a solution having a higher concentration of chloride is left behind. The concentration of chloride here is around 105 mEq/L.

In the second half of the proximal tubule, sodium gets re-absorbed along with chloride since there is only a little glucose and amino acids yet to be re-absorbed. The second half of the proximal tubule has a concentration of chloride ≈140 mEq/L. This higher chloride concentration favors its own diffusion from the lumen into the renal interstitial fluid.

Although the amount of sodium in the tubular fluid decreases markedly along the proximal tubule, the concentration of sodium and the total osmolarity remain relatively constant. This is because the proximal tubule is highly permeable to water and water reabsorption increases to keep pace with the sodium reabsorption.
questions.learning: Chloride — The concentration of chloride on the luminal side is more when compared to sodium, glucose, and amino acids. In the first half of the proximal tubule, sodium is reabsorbed by co-transport along with glucose, amino acids, and other solutes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old female patient comes to the outpatient department with complaints of neck swelling. She gives a history of weight loss and palpitations. On examination, she has exophthalmos and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland. Which of the following is not true?
options: Severe disease can cause vision loss
NO SPECS criteria is used for this condition
10% of isolated cases is present without hyperthyroidism
Condition will improve simultaneously with improvement in thyrotoxic state
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Condition will improve simultaneously with improvement in thyrotoxic state

The given clinical scenario of a female patient presenting with neck swelling weight loss, palpitations, exophthalmos, and diffusely enlarged thyroid gland is suggestive of Graves' disease with thyroid eye disease. Thyroid eye disease (TED) does not improve simultaneously with improvement in the thyrotoxic state.

Graves’ disease causes hyperthyroidism through thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) synthesized by lymphocytes in the thyroid gland, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. TSI antibodies stimulate the thyroid gland, causing hyperthyroidism.

Symptoms include hyperactivity, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations, weakness, weight loss, increased appetite, and diarrhoea. Signs include tachycardia, goitre, tremor, muscle weakness, and atrial fibrillation in the elderly.

Thyroid ophthalmopathy is seen in one-third of patients with Grave’s disease. Thyroid dermopathy usually occurs in the presence of moderate or severe ophthalmopathy. It primarily manifests as noninflamed, indurated plaques with a deep pink or purple colour and an "orange skin" appearance, commonly found on the anterior and lateral aspects of the lower leg (pretibial myxedema).

Investigations done on a patient with Graves' disease include:

• Thyroid function tests- TSH levels are decreased with or without elevated T3 and T4 levels.
• Anti-thyroid antibodies—Elevated levels of TSH receptor antibodies are diagnostic of Graves' disease. Other antibodies, like anti-Tg and anti-TPO, are elevated in most patients.
• Ultrasound of the neck is performed to evaluate vascularity, echogenicity, nodules, and clinical landmarks for surgical planning.
• A radioactive iodine uptake (RAIU) scan (thyroid scan) should be performed and a diffuse uptake confirms the diagnosis of Graves' disease. It is also useful to differentiate TSI-negative Graves disease from toxic nodular disease based on diffuse or nodular uptake patterns.
• CT or MRI scans of the orbits are useful to evaluate Graves’ ophthalmopathy.

Hyperthyroidism can be treated by antithyroid drugs, radioiodine treatment (I131), or thyroidectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Severe disease can cause vision loss mainly due to compression of the optic nerve at the orbit's apex, which can result in peripheral field defects, papilledema, and, in the worst case scenario, irreversible blindness.

Option B: NO SPECS scoring system as described below can be used to evaluate ophthalmopathy.

• No signs or symptoms
• Only signs (lid retraction, or lag)
• Soft tissue involvement (periorbital oedema)
• Proptosis
• Extraocular muscle involvement
• Corneal involvement
• Sight loss

Option C: 10% of isolated cases of thyroid eye disease are present without hyperthyroidism as they may also present as euthyroid or hypothyroid.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a rapidly enlarging mass arising from the uterine wall along with perimenopausal bleeding. Histopathological examination suggests a malignant tumor of smooth muscle origin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Leiomyosarcoma

A rapidly enlarging uterine mass in a perimenopausal woman, especially when accompanied by abnormal uterine bleeding, should raise suspicion for leiomyosarcoma. Histologically, leiomyosarcoma is a malignant smooth muscle tumor characterized by marked cytologic atypia, high mitotic activity (typically ≥10 mitoses/10 HPF), and tumor cell necrosis. Unlike leiomyoma, it arises de novo rather than from malignant transformation of a pre-existing fibroid.

• Spread: Predominantly hematogenous, most commonly to the lungs
• Immunohistochemistry: Desmin+, Smooth Muscle Actin (SMA)+, H-caldesmon+

Why not the other options?

• A. Leiomyoma: Benign smooth muscle tumor with well-circumscribed borders, minimal atypia, low mitotic activity, and no coagulative tumor necrosis.
• B. Endometrial carcinoma: Malignancy of the endometrial glands; histology shows malignant glandular structures rather than spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells.
• C. Adenomyosis: Presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium causing dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia; it is a benign, non-neoplastic condition.
questions.learning: Leiomyosarcoma — A rapidly enlarging uterine mass in a perimenopausal woman, especially when accompanied by abnormal uterine bleeding, should raise suspicion for leiomyosarcoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency room with central chest pain and has a known history of heart disease. An ECG is provided. Based on the ECG findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The provided ECG demonstrates significant ST-segment elevation in the anterior leads (V2-V4) and lateral leads (I, aVL, V5, V6). Crucially, there is reciprocal ST-segment depression in the inferior leads (III and aVF), which is a hallmark finding that differentiates a myocardial infarction (MI) from other conditions like pericarditis. This pattern indicates an acute injury involving the anterior wall (supplied by the LAD) and the lateral wall (supplied by the LCX or diagonal branches). Inferolateral MI (Option B) is incorrect because it would require ST elevation in inferior leads, whereas they show depression here. Acute pericarditis (Option C) typically presents with diffuse ST elevation across most leads and lacks localized reciprocal changes. Constrictive pericarditis (Option D) is a chronic condition characterized by low voltage QRS or nonspecific changes rather than acute ST elevation. Thus, the localized elevations and reciprocal depressions confirm an Anterolateral MI

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a translucent, bluish cystic swelling in the oral cavity, suggestive of a ranula, which is a mucus-filled cyst typically caused by salivary gland obstruction. Which site is the most common location for the development of a ranula?
questions.explanation: A ranula is a clinical term for a large mucocele specifically located on the floor of the mouth. It most frequently originates from the sublingual salivary gland, though it can occasionally involve the submandibular duct. The anatomical floor of the mouth provides the space where extravasated mucus can accumulate, forming the classic bluish, translucent, "frog-belly" cystic mass. Sites such as the tonsil (Option B), uvula (Option C), and cingula (Option D) are not associated with the development of ranulae. While mucoceles can occur on the lips or buccal mucosa, the term "ranula" is reserved exclusively for those occurring in the sublingual space. Understanding the site of origin is essential for surgical management, which often requires excision of the cyst along with the offending sublingual gland to prevent recurrence. Therefore, given the physiological and anatomical context of mucus retention cysts, the floor of the mouth is the definitive common site for ranula presentation
questions.learning: A ranula is a clinical term for a large mucocele specifically located on the floor of the mouth. It most frequently originates from the sublingual salivary gland, though it can occasionally involve the submandibular duct.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after choking on a bone while eating. He is conscious but unable to speak. What should be the immediate next step in management?
options: Deliver 5 back slaps and 5 chest compressions
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits a complete airway obstruction, indicated by the inability to speak or cough while remaining responsive. For a responsive adult or adolescent with a foreign body airway obstruction, the "Heimlich maneuver" (subdiaphragmatic abdominal thrusts) is the recommended immediate intervention to expel the object. Back slaps and chest compressions (Option A) are used for infants under one year of age, not adults. Endoscopic removal (Option B) is a definitive treatment for objects in the esophagus or bronchus but is not the first-line emergency step for a choking patient in respiratory distress. Bag and mask ventilation (Option C) will not work because the airway is mechanically blocked; it may actually push the object deeper. If the patient becomes unresponsive, the provider should start CPR, beginning with chest compressions, to relieve the obstruction

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient presents with abdominal pain, diarrhea, step-ladder–pattern fever, headache, and malaise, with symptoms progressively worsening over the past two weeks. Which diagnostic test is most appropriate to confirm the suspected condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with classical features of enteric (typhoid) fever, including step-ladder pattern fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, headache, and malaise progressing over two weeks. In such cases, the commonly used diagnostic test in many exam settings is the Widal test, which detects antibodies against Salmonella typhi (O and H antigens) in the patient’s serum. The Widal test becomes positive after the first week of infection, making it useful in patients presenting in the second week, as in this case. It is widely used in clinical practice, especially in resource-limited settings, and is often considered the expected answer in theoretical examinations. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Stool culture → Positive in later stages (3rd week) (C) Blood culture → Best in early disease but may take time and may not always be positive later (D) Urine culture → Not specific for typhoid diagnosis

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The best type of anesthesia for pre eclampsia is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Epidural anesthesia

Continuous epidural anesthesia is the first choice for most patients with preeclampsia during labor, vaginal delivery, and cesarean section.

Pre-eclampsia patients have a risk of severe airway edema, which makes intubation difficult. Thus continuous epidural anesthesia is advantageous as it avoids the need for intubation. Besides, continuous epidural anesthesia can improve uteroplacental perfusion and also decrease catecholamine secretion.

But one major prerequisite for regional anesthesia in preeclamptic patients is normal platelet count and normal coagulation. Coagulopathy is a contraindication for regional anesthesia.

Minimal platelet count for regional anesthesia is 100,000/μL, but some cases can be taken up with a platelet count as low as 70,000/μL.

General anesthesia is indicated in patients with coagulopathy and in severe pre-eclampsia with complications.

Spinal anesthesia can be given in mild pre-eclampsia but hypotension associated with spinal anesthesia limits its use in moderate to severe pre-eclampsia.

Since the severity of pre-eclampsia or the type of delivery (vaginal or cesarean) is not mentioned, epidural anesthesia has an advantage over other techniques for above-mentioned reasons. Hence the best option here would be epidural anesthesia.
questions.learning: Epidural anesthesia Continuous epidural anesthesia is the first choice for most patients with preeclampsia during labor, vaginal delivery, and cesarean section.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Gastric lavage is contraindicated in which of the following poisonings?
questions.explanation: Gastric lavage ("pumping the stomach") is a common decontamination procedure, but it is strictly contraindicated in hydrocarbon poisoning (e.g., kerosene, gasoline, or thinner). These substances have low viscosity and high volatility. During the process of lavage or vomiting, they can easily be aspirated into the lungs, where even a tiny amount can cause a severe, life-threatening chemical pneumonitis. Lavage is also contraindicated in corrosive (acid/alkali) poisoning due to the risk of esophageal perforation. Strychnine (Option A) and Paraldehyde (Option B) poisonings can be managed with lavage if done early. For iron tablet poisoning (Option D), whole bowel irrigation is often preferred over simple lavage because the tablets are large and heavy and difficult to remove through a tube. In hydrocarbon cases, management is purely supportive, and inducing vomiting must be avoided at all costs to protect the patient's airway
questions.learning: Gastric lavage ("pumping the stomach") is a common decontamination procedure, but it is strictly contraindicated in hydrocarbon poisoning (e.g., kerosene, gasoline, or thinner).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Cellular junctions present in a cardiac muscle are all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Zonula occludens

Zonula occludens is the other name for the tight junction. It is absent in a cardiac muscle.

Cardiac muscle cells are connected by Fascia adherens (a structural analog of zonula adherens), Gap junctions and Macula adherens.

Cardiac muscle fibers are made up of many individual cells connected in series and parallel to one another. The areas where the end of one muscle fiber abuts on another are called intercalated disks. At each intercalated disc, the plasma membrane fuses with one another forming gap junction which provides low resistance bridges for the spread of excitation from one fiber to another permitting the cardiac muscle to function as a syncytium.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department after being sexually assaulted by a neighbor. On evaluation, the police confirm that the accused was entrusted with the child's care while her parents were away. Under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, this incident is classified as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aggravated sexual assault

Aggravated sexual assault under the POCSO Act, 2012 refers to sexual assault committed under specific aggravating circumstances, such as when the offender:

• Is a person in a position of trust or authority (e.g., relative, teacher, guardian, caregiver).
• Is a police officer, member of the armed forces, or public servant.
• Is a staff member of a hospital, educational institution, or child care institution.
• Causes grievous hurt, disability, or life-threatening injury to the child.
• Commits the offence during communal violence, natural disasters, or similar situations of vulnerability.

In this case, the accused was entrusted with the child's care, making it an aggravated sexual assault.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following options is false regarding the measurement of temperature in a febrile patient?
options: Rectal temperature is ideal for measuring the core body temperature
Rectal temperature is lower than axillary temperature
Tympanic membrane temperature is lower than rectal temperature
Rectal temperature is higher than oral temperature.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rectal temperature is lower than axillary temperature

With regards to the measurement of temperature in a febrile patient, rectal temperature is higher than axillary temperature.

For humans, the conventional normal value for oral temperature is 37°C (98.6°F).

Rectal temperature represents the core body temperature and is less affected by changes in environmental temperature. It remains relatively constant. In comparison, oral temperature is typically 0.5°C lower than rectal temperature. However, the oral temperature can be influenced by various factors such as consuming hot or cold fluids, chewing gum, smoking, and breathing through the mouth.

Tympanic membrane thermometers measure radiant heat emitted by the tympanic membrane and the nearby ear canal, providing an absolute value of temperature. Tympanic membrane readings are generally 0.8°C (1.6°F) lower than rectal temperatures. The axillary temperature measured is lower than the rectal temperature.
questions.learning: Rectal temperature is lower than axillary temperature With regards to the measurement of temperature in a febrile patient, rectal temperature is higher than axillary temperature.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A case involving the death of a married woman within three years of marriage is reported. Who is responsible for conducting the inquest in this case?
questions.explanation: In India, according to Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a Magisterial Inquest is mandatory in cases involving the death of a woman within seven years of her marriage under suspicious circumstances. Since this case involves a death within three years of marriage, it falls strictly under the purview of a Magistrate (Executive or Judicial) to investigate potential foul play, such as dowry death or homicide. A Police Inquest (Option B) is the standard procedure for most unnatural deaths, but it is superseded by the Magistrate in this specific legal context. "Judicial" (Option A) is a broad term; while a Judicial Magistrate can perform the inquest, the correct specific authority is the Magistrate. The Coroner system (Option C) does not exist in modern India, as its functions were replaced by the Magisterial system. Therefore, a Magistrate must conduct the inquiry to ensure a thorough and impartial legal investigation
questions.learning: In India, according to Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), a Magisterial Inquest is mandatory in cases involving the death of a woman within seven years of her marriage under suspicious circumstances.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young boxer receives a blow near the eye during a boxing match. He presents to the ER with hematoma around eye, CT scan is shown below. Identify the radiological sign shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Tear-drop sign

The given CT image dipicts 'tear-drop' sign and suggests a blowout fracture.

Tear-drop/ hanging drop sign is characteristic of an orbital "blow-out" fracture, which represents the orbital contents herniating through the floor of the orbit into the maxillary antrum. The most useful projection for detecting an orbital floor fracture is Water’s view.

An orbital blow-out fracture is an isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blow out fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum. Clinical signs are periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival haemorrhage (later stages).

Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Indications for surgery in a blowout fracture include diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma, a fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum, incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in globe retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze and enophthalmos. If any of these conditions are present, surgical correction is required within 2 weeks.

The below-given X-ray image in the Water's view shows a 'tear-drop' sign

The optimal time for surgery following a blow-out fracture is 10–14 days.

Indications for surgery in a "blow-out" fracture are as follows:

* Diplopia not resolving significantly in the early days after trauma

* A fracture with a large herniation of tissues into the antrum

* Incarceration of tissues in the fracture, resulting in  globe  retraction and increased applanation tension on attempted upward gaze

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

Other options:

Option A: Panda sign: A radiological finding in sarcoidosis showing bilateral symmetrical uptake in the lacrimal and parotid glands on gallium scan, creating an appearance resembling a panda's face.

Option B: Dalrymple’s sign is the commonest and earliest sign of Grave's ophthalmopathy. It is due to overactivity of levator aponeurosis and Müller's muscle. Here the upper lid margin is at level with or above the superior limbus, causing the upper sclera to become visible (scleral show).

Option C: Munson's sign is seen in keratoconus. There is a localized bulging of the lower eyelid that can be seen in a downward-looking eye.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child was brought to the emergency with drooling and choking following ingestion of a foreign body. Based on the given X-ray, what object was most likely swallowed by the child?
options: Cap of a cool drink bottle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Button battery

The presence of a halo sign or double ring sign is indicative of the foreign body being a button battery. Furthermore, the presence of irregularities along the periphery of the battery indicates the possibility of corrosion.

Button batteries and sharp objects in the oesophagus and foreign bodies associated with respiratory symptoms all mandate urgent endoscopic removal.

Button batteries, in particular, are very dangerous foreign bodies, which must be expediently removed because they can cause:

• Mucosal injury in 1-hour contact time
• Involve all layers of the oesophagus in 4 hours

Injury is thought to be secondary to electrochemical burns from electrical discharge. Chemical burns from electrolyte alkali leakage and pressure necrosis also may contribute to mucosal injury.

Asymptomatic blunt objects and coins lodged in the oesophagus can be observed for up to 24 hr in anticipation of passage into the stomach.

Another AP and lateral X-ray demonstrating the presence of a button battery in the oesophagus is as shown below.
questions.learning: Button battery — The presence of a halo sign or double ring sign is indicative of the foreign body being a button battery. Furthermore, the presence of irregularities along the periphery of the battery indicates the possibility of corrosion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of sudden onset headache, palpitation, and profuse sweating. The patient has had multiple similar episodes in the past. During these episodes, the patient's blood pressure is elevated. A 24-hour urinary metanephrine is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pheochromocytoma

The most likely diagnosis in this patient is pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor of the sympathetic system arising from the adrenal medulla. Patients commonly present with a classical triad of palpitation, headache, and profuse sweating. Patients also present with hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias. These symptoms are due to an excess of catecholamines secreted by the tumor.

Other options:

Option A: Addison's disease is a primary adrenal insufficiency in which the adrenal is unable to secrete adequate amounts of cortisol (glucocorticoid), and aldosterone (mineralocorticoid). The features are fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, low blood pressure, postural hypotension, hypoglycemia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, salt craving, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.

Option B: Renal artery stenosis is a relatively common finding in older patients with chronic essential hypertension. However, it is clinically significant (i.e. renovascular hypertension) only if the stenosis is greater than 75% in both renal arteries or 50% stenosis with post-stenotic dilatation. Main causes include atherosclerosis (most common), usually seen in patients > 45 years and fibromuscular dysplasia, seen in women < 50 years.

Option D: Hyperthyroidism presents with clinical features that include heat intolerance and sweating, tachycardia, and palpitations, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhea, and oligomenorrhea. Clinical findings include exophthalmos, tremors, and myopathy.

Pearl PF1539: Pheochromocytoma

Features:

* When pheochromocytoma is associated with the MEN syndrome it is rarely malignant.

* Phaeochromocytomas are greyish-pink on the cut surface and are usually highly vascularised.

* Zellbalen cells and nuclei with salt and pepper chromatin are seen.

Factors indicating more chances of malignancy:

* An increased PASS (phaeochromocytoma of the adrenal gland scale score)

* High number of Ki-67-positive cells

* Vascular invasion or a breached capsule

Diagnosis:

* Urinary catecholamine and VMA level assay are most sensitive screening test.

* MRI is the IOC.

* Biopsy and CT Contrast scan are contraindicated in order to avoid Hypertensive crisis.

Treatment:

* Adrenalectomy is preferred TOC.

* Size<5 cm -  Laparoscopic adrenalectomy

* Preop Alpha blockers should be given

* Mitotane should be started as adjuvant or palliative treatment

Pearl PF0131: Clinical features of Pheochromocytoma (By frequency of occurrence)

* Clinical triad:

* Headaches – M/C symptom

* Profuse sweating

* Palpitations and tachycardia

* Hypertension, sustained or paroxysmal – M/C Sign

* Anxiety and panic attacks

* Weight loss

* Polyuria and polydipsia

* Constipation

* Orthostatic hypotension

* Dilated cardiomyopathy

* Erythrocytosis

* Elevated blood sugar

* Hypercalcemia
questions.learning: Pheochromocytoma — The most likely diagnosis in this patient is pheochromocytoma. Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumor of the sympathetic system arising from the adrenal medulla.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Four weeks after cataract surgery, a patient presents with pain, decreased vision, and redness in the eye. Examination reveals cells in the anterior chamber and vitreous haze. Identify the diagnosis and the associated microorganism:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Endophthalmitis; Staph epidermidis

Postoperative endophthalmitis is an acute, sight-threatening intraocular infection occurring after procedures like cataract surgery, presenting with pain, decreased vision, redness, anterior chamber reaction, and vitreous haze.

• Most common organism for early endophtalmitis (<6 weeks) : Staphylococcus epidermidis (normal conjunctival flora); P.acnes >6 weeks
• Infection involves both anterior chamber and vitreous → differentiates from sterile inflammation

Clinical differentiation:

• Endophthalmitis:

• Painful
• Severe vision loss
• Vitreous involvement (haze)

• TASS (toxic anterior segment syndrome):

• Sterile, painless
• Limited to anterior segment only

Why not other options:

• Posterior capsular opacification: Painless, late complication
• Sympathetic ophthalmia: Bilateral autoimmune condition

questions.text: In a population of 30,000, there were 500 live births & 14 still births in the year 2023. There were 18 children that died before the age of 1 year, 12 before 28 days of life & among that, 9 died in the first 7 days of life. Calculate the early neonatal mortality rate?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 18

The early neonatal mortality rate here would be 18 per 1,000 live births.

It can be calculated as shown:

The neonatal mortality rate (NMR) refers to the rate of deaths within the first 28 days of life. It is calculated using the following parameters:

• Early neonatal deaths- death in the first 7 days of life
• Late neonatal deaths - after 7th day but before 28th completed day of life

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient underwent total laryngectomy for laryngeal cancer. Identify the modality of voice production in this patient shown in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tracheoesophageal prosthesis

The modality of voice production shown in the given image is a tracheoesophageal voice prosthesis.

In a tracheoesophageal prosthesis, the exhaled air from the trachea is diverted to the esophagus through a device that connects the trachea and esophagus. It has a one-way valve, which prevents food from entering into the trachea. A variety of tracheoesophageal prostheses are available including the provox, Blom-Singer, and Panje devices.

Other options:

Option A: Electrolarynx is a vibrating device that produces a low-pitched sound in the hypopharynx. It is then articulated by the palate, tongue, and teeth.

Option B: Chicago implant is a hearing aid.

Option D: In oesophageal speech, the patient is trained to swallow air and slowly release it into the pharynx. 6-10 words can be spoken in a rough manner before re-swallowing the air.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
questions.explanation: Intraductal papilloma is a benign tumor that forms within a milk duct and is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge. It typically presents in women aged 35–55 as a small, palpable lump near the nipple accompanied by clear or bloody discharge. Breast cancer (Option A) can also cause bloody discharge but is statistically less common than papilloma. Fibroadenoma (Option B) typically presents as a firm, painless, mobile mass in younger women and does not cause discharge. Duct ectasia (Option D) involves inflammation and dilation of the ducts; while it can cause greenish, blackish, or occasionally bloody discharge, it remains less frequent than papilloma. Diagnosis involves clinical examination, mammography, and biopsy to rule out malignancy. Management is usually surgical excision of the affected duct
questions.learning: Intraductal papilloma is a benign tumor that forms within a milk duct and is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge. It typically presents in women aged 35–55 as a small, palpable lump near the nipple accompanied by clear or bloody discharge.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The following image shows a health belief model. What does box C stand for?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Health motivation

Box C stands for health motivation.

The health belief model was proposed from the idea that a person's health behavior changes in accordance with certain beliefs.

It can be categorized as follows:

• Individual perceptions.
• Variable factors that modify beliefs.
• Action.

Individual perceptions:

Perceived susceptibility refers to a person's own beliefs about the probability of developing a disease. If the perceived susceptibility is high, an individual is more likely to engage in health-promoting behavior to reduce the chances of contracting the illness.

Perceived severity is an individual's assessment of the severity of a particular health problem. If the disease is perceived to have a high severity, then the person is more likely to adopt a healthier lifestyle.

Perceived threat comprises perceived susceptibility and severity. People with a higher perceived threat tend to take on health-promoting activities.

Action:

Perceived benefits refer to a person's subjective judgment on how a particular health habit is modifying his chances of developing a disease. If the person believes that a habit is likely to reduce his/her chances of susceptibility to a disease or lower the severity of a disease, he/she is more likely to follow that healthy habit.

Perceived barriers to action also influence if a person wants to follow healthy behavior. The benefits of a particular health habit must overweigh the barriers that a person must overcome to continue following that behavior.

Cues to action may be internal or external. Internal cues include pain and clinical symptoms. External cues include awareness through media, physicians, and friends.

Behavioral modification (Option B) is part of the action after assessing all of the above-mentioned concepts.

Self-efficacy (Option D) can be defined as a person's capacity in achieving his health goals. A person's confidence in his/her ability to overcome limitations to attain his/her health goals was found to be a major factor in determining the outcome of his behavioral changes.

The health belief system is thought to be useful in analyzing health behavior patterns and formulating disease prevention plans based on these beliefs. All internal and external factors, including demographic and psychological characteristics, aim at health motivation to attain the action phase of a health belief system.

Other options:

Option A: Perceived control refers to a person's internal belief in the control they would have over things that are part of the past or the future or over a process, behavior, and outcome. Perceived control can influence all of the categories of the health belief system.
questions.learning: Health motivation Box C stands for health motivation. The health belief model was proposed from the idea that a person's health behavior changes in accordance with certain beliefs.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A pediatrician is counseling new mothers about breastfeeding. Which of the following situations is considered an absolute contraindication to breastfeeding?
options: Infants born to an HbsAg-positive mother
questions.explanation: Breast milk is almost always the ideal nutrition, but classic galactosemia in the infant (Option B) is one of the few absolute contraindications. These infants lack the enzyme to metabolize galactose, a component of the lactose in breast milk. Continued exposure leads to liver failure, cataracts, and intellectual disability. HIV infection (Option C) is a contraindication in developed nations, but in many developing countries, the WHO recommends breastfeeding if safe formula alternatives are unavailable. Alcohol consumption (Option A) is a relative contraindication; mothers are advised to limit intake and timing. Infants of HbsAg-positive mothers (Option D) can safely breastfeed once they receive the Hepatitis B vaccine and immunoglobulin at birth. Therefore, because galactosemia represents a life-threatening metabolic inability to process any human milk, it is the definitive absolute contraindication listed. These infants must be fed specialized lactose-free formula
questions.learning: Breast milk is almost always the ideal nutrition, but classic galactosemia in the infant (Option B) is one of the few absolute contraindications. These infants lack the enzyme to metabolize galactose, a component of the lactose in breast milk.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 19-year-old male patient comes to the clinic for follow-up 3 weeks after a traumatic fracture in his right thigh. On examination, he was found to have a hard palpable mass near the fracture site. X-ray of the area shows the findings below. A histological section shows central fibrous tissue and mature bone at the periphery. Which of the following is true about this patient's diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Myositis ossificans

Key clues

• 19-year-old male
• History of trauma with fracture
• 3 weeks later → hard palpable mass near fracture site
• X-ray shows calcification in soft tissue
• Histology: central fibrous tissue with mature bone at the periphery

These findings are classic for Myositis Ossificans.

It is heterotopic bone formation in muscle, usually occurring after trauma.

Common features:

• Occurs weeks after injury
• Painful or firm mass
• Peripheral ossification on imaging

Classic Histology (Zonation phenomenon)

This is the key diagnostic feature:

| Zone | Finding

| ---- | -------

| Center | Immature fibroblasts / fibrous tissue

| Intermediate zone | Osteoid formation

| Periphery | Mature lamellar bone

X-ray shows: Peripheral calcification with central lucency

Other options:

A. Parosteal osteosarcoma

• Malignant tumor
• Shows central ossification

C. Osteochondroma

• Cartilage-capped bony projection
• Arises from metaphysis
• Continuous with cortex and medulla

D. AV fistula

• Vascular abnormality
• No bone formation.

|

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Most common organ infected with genital tuberculosis.
questions.explanation: In cases of female genital tuberculosis, the Fallopian tube is the most frequently affected organ, involved in approximately 90–100% of patients. The infection typically reaches the genital tract via hematogenous spread from a primary pulmonary focus. Following the tubes, the endometrium within the uterus is the next most common site, involved in about 50–60% of cases (Option D). The ovaries are affected in approximately 20–30% of instances (Option A), while the cervix (Option C) is a relatively rare site of involvement, seen in only 5–15% of cases. Genital tuberculosis is a significant cause of tubal factor infertility and chronic pelvic pain in endemic regions. The destruction of the endosalpinx leads to bilateral tubal block and hydrosalpinx, which can be visualized on hysterosalpingography. Diagnosis often requires endometrial biopsy or diagnostic laparoscopy with peritoneal fluid analysis

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An X-ray image of the elbow joint is shown. The most likely age of the individual is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 8–10 years

Age estimation from an elbow X-ray is based on the appearance of the secondary ossification centers, remembered by the mnemonic CRITOE.

CRITOE sequence of ossification:

| Ossification center | Approximate age of appearance (years)

| ------------------- | -------------------------------------

| C – Capitellum | 1

| R – Radial head | 3

| I – Internal (medial) epicondyle | 5

| T – Trochlea | 7

| O – Olecranon | 9

| E – External (lateral) epicondyle | 11

In this X-ray:

• Capitellum, radial head, medial epicondyle, and trochlea are ossified.
• Olecranon ossification center is present.
• Lateral epicondyle has not yet appeared/fused.

This corresponds to an age of approximately 8–10 years.

Why not the other options?

• B. 10–13 years: Lateral epicondyle (E) should also be visible.
• C. 14–16 years: Fusion of several epiphyses begins.
• D. 18–20 years: Complete fusion of elbow ossification centers is expected.
