questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly woman involved in a road traffic accident presents with respiratory distress and altered sensorium. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated D-dimer levels, and the chest X-ray demonstrates suggestive findings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of respiratory distress and altered mental status following a high-energy accident (likely involving long bone fractures) is diagnostic of Fat Embolism Syndrome. This occurs when fat globules from bone marrow are released into the bloodstream and travel to the lungs and brain. Respiratory distress usually manifests 24–72 hours after trauma due to capillary obstruction. Gas gangrene (Option A) presents with crepitus and foul discharge. Acute infection (Option C) typically presents with fever rather than sudden post-traumatic hypoxia. While pulmonary embolism (Option D) also causes respiratory distress and elevated D-dimer, it is less likely to cause early altered mental status or the classic petechial rash often seen in fat embolism. The suggestive X-ray likely shows bilateral patchy infiltrates mimicking ARDS, which is characteristic of this syndrome. Thus, fat embolism is the most consistent post-traumatic diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of respiratory distress and altered mental status following a high-energy accident (likely involving long bone fractures) is diagnostic of Fat Embolism Syndrome.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is tandem radiotherapy commonly used?
questions.explanation: Tandem radiotherapy (a form of brachytherapy) is a cornerstone in the treatment of cervical cancer. It involves the insertion of a hollow metal tube (the tandem) through the cervix into the uterine cavity, often combined with ovoids placed in the vaginal fornices (the "Tandem and Ovoids" technique). This allows for a very high dose of radiation to be delivered directly to the tumor site while sparing the surrounding healthy tissues like the bladder and rectum. Ovarian cancer (Option B) is primarily treated with surgery and systemic chemotherapy. Choriocarcinoma (Option C) is a highly chemosensitive malignancy where radiation is rarely used as a primary modality. While brachytherapy can be used for certain stages of endometrial cancer (Option D), the specific term "tandem" is most classically and frequently associated with the standard Fletcher-Suite or similar applicators used for cervical malignancy. Brachytherapy is critical for improving local control rates in cervical cancer

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the recommended method for the initial screening of cervical cancer among women at the primary health care level?
options: Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution
questions.explanation: In resource-limited settings like a Primary Health Center (PHC) in India, the most practical and effective screening method is "Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA)". This involves applying a 3% to 5% acetic acid solution to the cervix; pre-cancerous or cancerous lesions turn white ("aceto-white") and can be easily seen by a trained health worker. Colposcopy (Option B) and Cervical biopsy (Option C) are "confirmatory" tests performed at higher centers (District hospitals or Medical colleges) once a screening test is positive. High vaginal biopsy (Option D) is not a standard screening tool. VIA is preferred over the Pap smear at the primary level because it provides "immediate results," allows for the "see-and-treat" approach, and does not require complex laboratory infrastructure. Screening is recommended for women aged 30-65 to reduce mortality from this highly preventable cancer
questions.learning: In resource-limited settings like a Primary Health Center (PHC) in India, the most practical and effective screening method is "Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA)".

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 56-year-old woman presents with weight loss, newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus and a painful erythematous rash over the perineum and lower abdomen. Over the last 3 months she has also developed low mood with anhedonia and has been treated for a left lower limb deep vein thrombosis. Investigations show fasting plasma glucose of 212 mg/dL and markedly elevated fasting plasma glucagon levels. Which of the following clinical features is classically included in the “4 Ds” of glucagonoma syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermatitis

To recognize glucagonoma syndrome, a rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor characterized by the classic “4 Ds”:

1. Dermatitis – Necrolytic migratory erythema (NME)

o Painful erythematous rash in perineum, groin, lower abdomen, and extremities

o Most characteristic and diagnostic feature

2. Diabetes mellitus

o Due to excess glucagon causing hyperglycemia

3. Depression

o Neuropsychiatric symptoms including depression, lethargy

4. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

o Hypercoagulable state commonly seen

• Weight loss

• New-onset diabetes

• Necrolytic migratory erythema

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: After falling from a height onto his outstretched hand, a man is brought to the emergency department. Radiographic evaluation reveals a fracture of the clavicle. Which part of the clavicle is most commonly involved in such fractures?
questions.explanation: The clavicle is one of the most frequently fractured bones in the body, typically resulting from direct trauma or a fall on an outstretched hand. Statistically, the junction of the medial two-thirds and the lateral one-third (Option A) is the most common site of fracture. This region represents the anatomical weakest point of the bone, where the curvature changes and the bone is least reinforced by ligaments or muscle attachments. Approximately 80% of all clavicle fractures occur in this mid-shaft region. Fractures of the medial third (Option B and C) are relatively rare, often involving high-energy trauma. While the fracture is often described as being in the "middle" (Option D), the precise and medically standardized answer for the site of maximum weakness is the junction described in Option A. These fractures are usually managed conservatively with a broad-arm sling or a figure-of-eight bandage

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following occur during the beginning cough reflex?
options: Forced expiration against a closed glottis
Forced expiration against an open glottis
Forced inspiration against a closed glottis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Forced expiration against a closed glottis

| Phase | Event

| ----- | -----

| Inspiratory phase | Deep inspiration

| Compression phase | Forced expiration against closed glottis

| Expulsive phase | Sudden opening of glottis → explosive airflow

The cough reflex begins with deep inspiration followed by closure of the glottis.

This is followed by forced expiration against a closed glottis, generating high intrathoracic pressure.

Sudden opening of the glottis then expels air explosively to clear irritants.

Hence, forced expiration against a closed glottis marks the beginning of the cough reflex.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the treatment of choice for a 4-year-old boy presenting with generalized edema, urine analysis showing 4+ proteinuria, and a urine protein–creatinine ratio of 3?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with Nephrotic Syndrome, characterized by massive proteinuria and generalized edema. In children, approximately 90% of nephrotic syndrome cases are due to Minimal Change Disease, which is highly responsive to corticosteroids. The preferred initial treatment is oral Prednisolone (Option A) given at a dose of for 6 weeks, followed by a tapering course. Cyclophosphamide (Option B), Levamisole (Option C), and Cyclosporine (Option D) are second-line immunosuppressive agents reserved for patients who are "steroid-resistant," "steroid-dependent," or "frequent relapsers" . Starting these agents as the initial treatment would be inappropriate given the high likelihood of steroid responsiveness in a 4-year-old. Complete remission (disappearance of proteinuria) is usually achieved within the first few weeks of Prednisolone therapy. Therefore, corticosteroids remain the cornerstone and gold standard for the first-line management of childhood nephrotic syndrome

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A mother brought her 14-year-old mentally retarded child with complaints of joint pain and an irresistible urge to bite his fingers and lips. On investigation, his serum uric acid level was found to be elevated. The child is likely suffering from which disorder?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome

The clinical features—intellectual disability, self-mutilation (biting lips/fingers), joint pain, and hyperuricemia—are characteristic of Lesch–Nyhan syndrome.

• Deficiency of HGPRT (Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase)
• A key enzyme in the purine salvage pathway
• Impaired salvage of hypoxanthine and guanine → increased degradation to uric acid
• ↑ PRPP and ↓ IMP/GMP → ↑ de novo purine synthesis → further uric acid production

Clinical features explained:

• Hyperuricemia → gout, joint pain
• Neurological dysfunction → intellectual disability
• Self-mutilation behavior (classic hallmark)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Xanthine oxidase deficiency: ↓ uric acid (xanthinuria), not hyperuricemia
• Thymidylate synthetase defect: Affects DNA synthesis
• CPS II defect: Affects pyrimidine synthesis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with hematuria, and evaluation reveals a 2×2 cm bladder mass consistent with low-grade transitional cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: For a patient with a localized, small (2x2 cm), low-grade transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) of the bladder, the most appropriate initial management is a Transurethral Resection of the Bladder Tumor (TURBT). TURBT serves both a diagnostic and therapeutic purpose, allowing for complete removal of the visible tumor while providing a tissue sample for histological staging of the muscle layer. Radical resection with an ileal conduit (Option B) is reserved for muscle-invasive bladder cancer or high-grade refractory disease. Partial cystectomy (Option C) is rarely indicated and only for very specific, isolated tumor locations. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Option D) is standard for muscle-invasive disease but not for a low-grade, non-invasive mass. In low-grade TCC, a single post-operative dose of intravesical chemotherapy (like Mitomycin C) is often added to the TURBT to further reduce the risk of recurrence. Thus, TURBT remains the standard-of-care for managing early-stage, low-grade bladder malignancies

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the marked bond:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hydrogen bond

The marked bond represents a hydrogen bond between thymine and adenine.

The complementary nitrogenous bases of the 2 strands of the DNA double helix are linked by hydrogen bonds. Adenine and thymine are linked by two hydrogen bonds (A=T) whereas three hydrogen bonds are present between cytidine and guanine (C≡G). Van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions are present between the stacked adjacent base pairs.

A β-N-glycosidic bond is present between the nitrogenous base and deoxyribose sugar. C1 of deoxyribose/ribose sugar is joined covalently to N1 of pyrimidines and N9 of purines by β-N-glycosidic bond. An ester bond is present between the sugar and phosphate group of the same nucleotide. An acid anhydride bond is present between two phosphate groups.

A polymer of nucleotides is joined by 3’-5’ phosphodiester bond. The bond is present between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate group of another.
questions.learning: Hydrogen bond — The marked bond represents a hydrogen bond between thymine and adenine. The complementary nitrogenous bases of the 2 strands of the DNA double helix are linked by hydrogen bonds.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a child diagnosed with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), which of the following vaccines is contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. MMR vaccine

In Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID), live attenuated vaccines are contraindicated due to the risk of vaccine-derived infection.

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by severe deficiency of T lymphocytes, impaired B-cell function and markedly weakened immune response.

Because these patients have severely impaired immunity, they cannot safely handle live attenuated vaccines, which contain weakened but still replicating organisms. Thus, live vaccines are contraindicated in SCID.

MMR is a live vaccine, whereas IPV, Hepatitis B, and DTaP are inactivated or toxoid vaccines and are safe.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old woman presents with complaints of breathlessness and easy fatigability. Clinical examination reveals distended neck veins, and assessment of the jugular venous pulse shows prominent X and Y descents. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of elevated JVP with prominent "X" and "Y" descents is a hallmark of Constrictive Pericarditis. In this condition, the rigid, fibrotic pericardium limits diastolic filling, leading to high venous pressures and rapid atrial emptying during the early diastolic phase (the Y descent). This contrasts with Cardiac Tamponade (Option B), where the "Y" descent is characteristically blunted or absent because the high intrapericardial pressure prevents rapid ventricular filling. Dilated cardiomyopathy (Option C) typically shows symptoms of congestive heart failure without these specific JVP patterns. Restrictive cardiomyopathy (Option D) can mimic constriction, but the rapid "X" and "Y" descents are much more classic for pericardial disease. Other signs of constrictive pericarditis include Kussmaul’s sign and a pericardial knock on auscultation. Definitive diagnosis often requires imaging or cardiac catheterization showing "dip and plateau" hemodynamics

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The given post operative xray of a patient is shown below.What is the most common electrolyte abnormality associated with this conditon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypokalemia

The X-ray shows multiple air-fluid levels and dilatations of both the small and large intestine which is suggestive of paralytic ileus, a type of adynamic obstruction. The most common electrolyte abnormality seen is hypokalemia.

Paralytic ileus is an adynamic obstruction in which there is a failure of transmission of peristaltic waves secondary to neuromuscular failure (i.e., in the myenteric [Auerbach’s] and submucous [Meissner’s] plexuses). Since there are no rigorous contractions, there is no colicky pain.

Clinical features :

The resultant stasis leads to the following:

* Accumulation of fluid and gas in the bowel

* With associated distension: marked and tympanitic

* Vomiting (effortless)

* Absence of bowel sounds

* Absolute constipation

* Paralytic ileus takes on clinical significance if any of the following are observed at 72 hours after laparotomy:

* No return of bowel sounds on auscultation

* No passage of flatus

* Colicky pain is not a feature

* Radiologically, the abdomen shows gas-filled loops of the intestine with multiple fluid levels (if an erect film is felt necessary)

Treatment:

* Paralytic ileus is managed with the use of nasogastric suction and restriction of oral intake until bowel sounds and the passage of flatus return.

* Electrolyte balance must be maintained.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 7-year-old male child presented with an episode of convulsions that had been ongoing for 45 minutes. He has a past medical history of GTCS. What would be the most appropriate management in this case? GTCS - Generalized tonic–clonic seizure
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lorazepam followed by Levetiracetam

This scenario described above is of status epilepticus. The first drug used is Lorazepam to immediately control and stop the seizure, followed by  Levetiracetam once the acute phase is managed.

Status epilepticus refers to continuous seizures or repetitive, discrete seizures with impaired consciousness in the inter-ictal period. For practical purposes, status epilepticus is defined as any one of the following:

* Continuing seizures >5 minutes or

* No regaining of consciousness between 2 seizures.

The initial choice of therapy is a benzodiazepine, which includes either of the following:

* Intravenous lorazepam

* Intravenous diazepam

* Intramuscular midazolam- If IV access is not available

If the seizure still continues, we can repeat the above dose once again. If there is no response even after repeat doses, then a single dose of either of the antiepileptics can be given,

* Intravenous fosphenytoin

* Intravenous valproic acid

* Intravenous levetiracetam

If the seizure activity continues for 30 minutes even after administration of two doses of a benzodiazepine and an antiepileptic drug, it is known as refractory status epilepticus. This patient requires endotracheal intubation for ventilatory support. General anaesthesia is induced using continuous infusion of midazolam, propofol, or phenobarbital.

Management of status epilepticus:

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In case of a chemical injury to the eye, what is the immediate first step in the management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Copious irrigation with saline

Chemical injury to the eye is an absolute ocular emergency, and the immediate first step is copious irrigation with saline (or any clean fluid available).

• Chemicals (especially alkali) penetrate rapidly and cause ongoing tissue damage
• Immediate dilution and removal of the chemical limits severity of injury and improves prognosis

Key management principles:

• Start irrigation immediately (do NOT delay for history or examination)
• Use normal saline, Ringer lactate, or even clean water if nothing else is available
• Continue until ocular surface pH normalizes (≈ 7–7.4)
• Evert eyelids to remove retained particles

Why not others:

• Visual acuity, history, IOP measurement → important but only after irrigation
• Any delay worsens corneal and limbal damage

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Treatment of Grade I Meningioma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surgical excision

Treatment of Grade I Meningioma is Simple surgical excision.

Meningioma:

Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid. Meningiomas may be found along any of the external surfaces of the brain as well as within the ventricular system, where they arise from the stromal arachnoid cells of the choroid plexus.

Meningiomas are usually rounded masses with well-defined dural bases that compress the underlying brain but are easily separated from it. The surface of the mass is usually encapsulated by thin, fibrous tissue and may have a bosselated or polypoid appearance.

They may also grow en plaque, in which the tumor spreads in a sheetlike fashion along the surface of the dura.

WHO grading of meningiomas:

* Grade I - Most meningiomas fall under this category. For example - Syncytial, fibroblastic, transitional, psammomatous, secretory, microcytic.

* Simple surgical excision is the treatment.

* Grade II - They are also called atypical meningiomas. These have a higher rate of recurrence and more aggressive growth. For example- Clear cell and chordoid type of meningiomas.

* These may require radiotherapy in addition to surgery.

* Grade III - These are called anaplastic (malignant) meningiomas and are highly aggressive tumors - Papillary and rhabdoid meningiomas are examples. Surgical excision of the tumor and the tissue it has invaded is the mainstay.

* Radiotherapy is an additional treatment. The recurrence rate is high even after tumor excision.
questions.learning: Surgical excision Treatment of Grade I Meningioma is Simple surgical excision. Meningioma: Meningiomas are predominantly benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura, that arise from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding single exposure point source epidemic ?
options: Has more than one incubation period
Occurs due to prolonged exposure to an agent
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Explosive in nature

The true statement regarding single exposure point source epidemic is that it is explosive in nature.

Single exposure point source epidemics occur due to a brief and simultaneous exposure to an agent. It has the following characteristics:

* It has a single peak with no secondary waves.

* The epidemic tends to be explosive, there is a clustering of cases within a narrow interval of time.

* The epidemic curve has a sharp, rapid rise and fall as all cases are clustered within one incubation period.

The exposure can be an infectious agent or contaminant in the environment (air, water, food, soil) by industrial chemicals or pollutants. Examples are food poisoning and the Bhopal gas tragedy in India due to methyl isocyanate.

The following graph represents single exposure point source epidemic.

Pearl PF0959: Epidemics and its Types

Epidemics and its Types

An epidemic is an occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness that is clearly in excess of normal expectancy.

Types

Common source epidemics

* Single exposure or 'point source' epidemics

* Multiple or continuous exposure epidemics

Propagated epidemics

* Person to person

* Arthropod vector

* Animal reservoir

Slow or modern epidemics

* Non-communicable diseases
questions.learning: Explosive in nature — The true statement regarding single exposure point source epidemic is that it is explosive in nature. Single exposure point source epidemics occur due to a brief and simultaneous exposure to an agent.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The given image is of a person with a history of minor trauma with a piece of wood, 20 days back. His face is affected on the left side with facial swelling and orbital edema. CT scan revealed clear sinuses and the presence of subcutaneous nodules. Microscopy of the tissue sections was PAS-positive and stained positive with Grocott's methenamine silver stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phycomycosis

The history of facial swelling and orbital edema following trauma with wood and positive fungal stain (Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver) points toward phycomycosis (mucormycosis), a potentially invasive fungal infection.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis caused by various molds in the Mucorales order which are ubiquitous thermotolerant saprobes. These molds, including Rhizopus, Mucor, and Absidia, are common in the environment. The spores can be found in air and dust.

Mucormycosis can manifest as a localized cutaneous or subcutaneous infection in immunologically normal individuals after traumatic exposure to soil or vegetation. It is a fatal condition due to its angio-invasive nature. Lung involvement is common, and the infection primarily affects immunocompromised patients.

Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is frequently seen in individuals with diabetic ketoacidosis. It typically starts with eye and facial pain and may progress to orbital cellulitis, proptosis, and vision loss. A characteristic finding is a black necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity.

Diagnosis involves testing specimens and cultures. In exudate samples, wet preparations with 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) reveal broad, ribbon-like hyphae. Tissue biopsy confirms the diagnosis by observing non-septate hyphae branching at right angles, characteristic of Mucorales like Rhizopus delemar.

Culture isolation is performed on Sabouraud agar without cycloheximide, resulting in grey-white colonies with a thick cottony, and fluffy surface.

Treatment is primarily with liposomal amphotericin B. Surgical debridement of the affected tissues and control of underlying predisposing cause is equally important.

Other options:

Option D: IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is characterized by tissue infiltrates dominated by IgG4 antibodies, which is the hallmark of the disease. IgG4-RD leads to fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis. Patients may present with Riedel's thyroiditis, autoimmune pancreatitis, or idiopathic orbital inflammation, but not with ptosis. Diagnosis is confirmed through positive fibrosis and the presence of plasma cells on biopsy. Treatment with Rituximab is done.

Option C: Foreign body granulomas are due to inflammation induced by inert foreign bodies. These granulomas develop without T-cell-mediated immune responses. Sutures are a common site for their formation. The foreign material is at the center of the granuloma, surrounded by epithelioid cells and specific giant cells opposing the surface.

Option B: Midline lethal granuloma is characterized by necrotizing destruction and damage to the nose and other respiratory structures. It is rare and usually a diagnosis of exclusion. CT scans can detect the lesions associated with this condition. Negative c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies) and fungal stain results contribute to the diagnosis.
questions.learning: Phycomycosis — The history of facial swelling and orbital edema following trauma with wood and positive fungal stain (Grocott-Gomori's methenamine silver) points toward phycomycosis (mucormycosis), a potentially invasive fungal infection.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
A 40-year-old woman presents with mild, progressive, bilateral hearing loss. A PTA showed the following findings. What is the most likely clinical finding in this patient?

PTA - Pure Tone Audiogram
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Schwartze sign

The clinical scenario describes a 40-year-old female patient with mild, progressive, bilateral hearing loss, and a PTA showing Carhart's notch (dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz) are all suggestive of Otosclerosis and the classical sign seen here is Schwartze sign.

The presence of a reddish hue on the promontory through the tympanic membrane, known as the Schwartze sign, suggests an active focus.

Otosclerosis is caused by bony overgrowth involving the enchondral layer of the bony otic capsule. It presents with bilateral progressive conductive hearing loss and tinnitus. It has an autosomal dominant inheritance and can worsen with stress and hormonal changes like during pregnancy and menopause.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fistula ante fenestrae.

PTA shows loss of air conduction with air-bone gap, more for lower frequencies and Carhart's notch may be seen. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage. Definitive treatment is stapedectomy/stapedotomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Carhart notch usually disappears after a successful stapedectomy.

Other options:

Option A: Hennebert sign is pressure-induced dizziness seen in patients with Superior semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome, congenital syphilis, and Méniére’s disease.

Option B: Compression of the facial nerve due to acoustic neuroma will result in hypoesthesia of the posterior wall of the external auditory canal. This is called the Hitzelberger sign.

Option D: The gurgling sound produced on pressing the swelling in the laryngocele is known as Bryce's sign.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which vaccines should healthcare workers receive?
questions.explanation: Healthcare workers (HCWs) are at significant occupational risk for blood-borne infections. Vaccination against Hepatitis B is the most critical and universally recommended immunization for all HCWs who may come into contact with blood or body fluids. The Hepatitis B vaccine is highly effective and prevents a leading cause of chronic liver disease and cirrhosis among medical professionals. Cholera (Option A) and Rabies (Option D) vaccines are generally only recommended for specialized workers, such as those in labs or endemic travel regions, rather than for general HCWs. HPV (Option B) is a routine vaccine for adolescents but is not an occupational requirement for HCWs. In addition to Hepatitis B, HCWs should ideally be immune to influenza, measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella. Occupational safety standards mandate that employers provide the Hepatitis B vaccine free of charge to at-risk staff. This protective measure is fundamental to reducing the risk of workplace-acquired infections and ensuring the long-term health of the medical workforce
questions.learning: Healthcare workers (HCWs) are at significant occupational risk for blood-borne infections. Vaccination against Hepatitis B is the most critical and universally recommended immunization for all HCWs who may come into contact with blood or body fluids.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with worsening cough, progressive breathlessness, reduced exercise tolerance, and imaging evidence of pulmonary fibrosis. Which medication is appropriate for the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary fibrosis, particularly Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), is a progressive, irreversible lung disease characterized by scarring of the lung tissue. This leads to symptoms of chronic dry cough and exertional dyspnea as the lungs become stiff and oxygen exchange is impaired. Pirfenidone is one of the few FDA-approved antifibrotic medications specifically indicated to slow the progression of IPF. It works by inhibiting TGF-beta, a key pro-fibrotic cytokine, thereby reducing fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis. Bortezomib (Option A) is a proteasome inhibitor used for multiple myeloma. Roflumilast (Option B) is a PDE4 inhibitor used to reduce exacerbations in severe COPD. Imatinib (Option C) is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor primarily used for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) and Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST). While none of these drugs can cure or reverse the existing fibrosis, pirfenidone has been clinically proven to significantly decline the rate of loss of forced vital capacity (FVC) in these patients, thereby improving survival and quality of life
questions.learning: Pulmonary fibrosis, particularly Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF), is a progressive, irreversible lung disease characterized by scarring of the lung tissue.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 4-month-old breastfed infant develops failure to thrive, jaundice, and hepatomegaly. Slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral cataracts. Urine testing shows a reducing substance that is non-glucose. Which enzyme deficiency explains this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency

Classic galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency) causes accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate AND upstream galactose, which is shunted via aldose reductase to galactitol — this alcohol sugar deposits in the lens, causing infantile cataracts. This is distinct from isolated galactokinase deficiency, which also causes galactitol-mediated cataracts but with a comparatively milder overall systemic presentation (no hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, or E. coli sepsis risk), since galactose-1-phosphate itself does not accumulate to toxic levels in galactokinase deficiency.

| Feature | Classic galactosemia

| ------- | --------------------

| Enzyme deficient | Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase

| Toxic accumulation | Galactose-1-phosphate, galactitol

| Cataract mechanism | Galactose → galactitol (via aldose reductase) → lens deposition

| Additional risks | Failure to thrive, jaundice, hepatomegaly, intellectual disability, E. coli sepsis

| Treatment | Exclude galactose AND lactose from diet

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following acts by causing both decreased bone resorption and increased bone formation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Strontium ranelate

Strontium ranelate acts by both decreased bone resorption and increased bone formation.

It is generally reserved for severe osteoporosis. Due to an increased incidence of myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular events, the use is restricted in all the approved regions.

Option B- Ibandronate which is a bisphosphonate, decreases bone resorption only.

Option C- The pharmacologic activity of teriparatide, which is similar to the physiologic activity of PTH, includes stimulating osteoblast function, increasing gastrointestinal calcium absorption, and increasing renal tubular reabsorption of calcium.

Option D- Calcitonin also decreases bone resorption.
questions.learning: Strontium ranelate Strontium ranelate acts by both decreased bone resorption and increased bone formation. It is generally reserved for severe osteoporosis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer presented with a traumatic ulcer in his right eye. Microscopy was done which showed septate hyphae. What is the likely causative agent?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Aspergillus

The most likely causative agent based on the clinical features and microscopy showing septate hyphae given is Aspergillus.

Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common pathogenic species. It can cause invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. This can be due to prolonged treatment with steroids or retro-positive status. It starts as pneumonia, which can later spread to involve other organs. Voriconazole is the drug of choice.

Other manifestations include allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis where central bronchiectasis is usually seen. Aspergilloma and superficial infections like otomycosis or mycotic keratitis are the other presentations.

Histopathological examination of the tissue section shows characteristic septate hyphae with dichotomous branching at an acute angle. The hyphae stain poorly with hematoxylin and eosin, so periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stain is used.

Other methods for diagnosis include detection of galactomannan (Aspergillus cell-wall component) and culture isolation. Aspergillus fumigatus grows dark green colonies, while Aspergillus niger appears black. Yellow-green colonies are seen in case of Aspergillus flavus. Microscopic examination of colonies stained with lactophenol cotton blue would show septate hyphae and conidiophores.

Other options:

Options A and B - Rhizopus and Mucor are zygomycetes that are responsible for mucormycosis. Non-septate, broad hyphae are seen on tissue samples stained with hematoxylin and eosin.

The image below shows broad aseptate and irregularly-branched non-septate hyphae of Mucor.

Option C - Candida, the causative agent for candidiasis, appear as budding gram-positive cells on wet films and smears. Mycelial forms suggest colonization. Culture colonies are creamy-white and have a yeasty odor. Candida albicans, the most commonly implicated pathogenic species, form chlamydospores on corn meal agar.

The image below shows candidal hyphae and chlamydospores.
questions.learning: Aspergillus — The most likely causative agent based on the clinical features and microscopy showing septate hyphae given is Aspergillus. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common pathogenic species.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following effects of puberty are not mediated by estrogen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hair growth

Pubarche or the development of axillary and pubic hair is not mediated by estrogen. It occurs due to testosterone in both sexes. Around 50% of testosterone comes from the ovaries and the rest from the adrenal gland.

Puberty in girls involves breast development (thelarche), an increase in adrenal androgen secretion (adrenarche), and the beginning of menstrual cycles (menarche).

Estrogen has the following actions during puberty:

• Breast development
• Development of the reproductive tract
• Starting of menstruation (option D)
• Increased fat in the hips
• Regulation of pubertal growth spurt
• Vaginal cornification (option C)
• Cervical mucus production (option B)
• Epiphyseal closure
• Maintenance of bone formation - acts against parathyroid hormone.
questions.learning: Hair growth Pubarche or the development of axillary and pubic hair is not mediated by estrogen. It occurs due to testosterone in both sexes.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not included in the qSOFA score components?
questions.explanation: The quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score is a bedside tool designed to identify patients outside of the ICU who are at high risk for poor outcomes due to suspected sepsis. It consists of exactly three clinical components: Respiratory rate breaths per minute (Option A) Altered mental status (Glasgow Coma Scale ) (Option C) Systolic blood pressure mmHg (Option D) LDH (Option B) is NOT a component of the qSOFA score. While lactate is an important biomarker used in the full SOFA score and in defining septic shock, the qSOFA was specifically created to rely solely on physical exam findings and vital signs, requiring no laboratory tests at all for its calculation. A score of indicates a higher risk of prolonged ICU stay or in-hospital mortality. Therefore, LDH is the correct "except" choice as it is a laboratory value

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A researcher is studying the difference in the incidence of asthma in children who are exposed to second-hand smoke and those who are not. If he wishes to express the additional incidence of asthma in the exposed children as a percentage, which of the following should he use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Attributable risk

The researcher may use attributable risk to express the increased incidence of asthma in the exposed children.

Attributable risk (AR) is the difference in incidence rates of disease (or death) between an exposed group and the non-exposed group. It is often expressed as a percentage. The terms "risk difference" or "cumulative incidence difference" refers to attributable risk.

Other Options:

Option B: Relative risk (RR) is the ratio of the incidence of the disease (or death) among exposed and the incidence among non-exposed.

Option C: Population-attributable risk is the incidence of the disease (or death) in the total population minus the incidence of disease (or death) among those who were not exposed to the suspected causal factor. Population attributable risk is measured by multiplying attributable risk with the population prevalence of exposure.

Option D: Odds ratio is a measure of the strength of association between a risk factor and outcome in case-control studies.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the context of solid organ transplantation, which transplanted organ has the highest rate of rejection?
questions.explanation: In the field of solid organ transplantation, the small intestine is associated with the highest incidence of rejection among all listed organs. This is primarily because the intestine is an "immunologically active" organ containing a large amount of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) and a high density of donor immune cells (Graft-versus-Host risk). Furthermore, the constant exposure to a diverse luminal microbiome increases the risk of infection and inflammation, which triggers the recipient's immune system. Lungs (Option A) also have a high rejection rate compared to the heart or kidneys, but the intestine remains the most challenging. The Kidney (Option C) and Heart (Option D) have relatively lower rates of acute rejection due to established immunosuppression protocols and the lower load of lymphoid tissue. Because of this high risk, intestinal transplant recipients require extremely high doses of immunosuppressive drugs and vigilant monitoring via frequent endoscopic biopsies to detect early signs of rejection

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During a study on gastrointestinal hormones, a volunteer is administered the hormone secreted by S cells. Which of the following changes most likely represent the effect of this hormone on gastric and duodenal secretions?
options: Gastric H+ increases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- no change
Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 decreased, Duodenal Cl- no change
Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- decreases
Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- increases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- decreases

S cells of the duodenum secrete secretin in response to acidic chyme entering the duodenum.

Major actions of secretin:

• ↓ Gastric acid (H⁺) secretion → inhibits parietal cells and gastrin release
• ↑ Pancreatic and duodenal bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) secretion → neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum
• ↓ Chloride (Cl⁻) secretion in pancreatic/duodenal fluid because Cl⁻ is exchanged for HCO₃⁻ via the Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ exchanger

Physiologic role:

• Protects the duodenal mucosa from acid
• Creates an optimal alkaline environment for pancreatic enzymes
questions.learning: Gastric H+ decreases, Duodenal HCO3 increased, Duodenal Cl- decreases S cells of the duodenum secrete secretin in response to acidic chyme entering the duodenum.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with fever, ear pain, and swelling behind the ear. The clinical image shows postauricular swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute mastoiditis

Acute mastoiditis is the most common intratemporal complication of acute otitis media (AOM). It results from spread of infection into the mastoid air cells and presents with fever, otalgia, postauricular pain, erythematous swelling, tenderness, and protrusion of the pinna.

The image shows postauricular erythematous swelling with outward displacement of the pinna, which is classic for acute mastoiditis.

Why not the other options?

• A. Perichondritis of the pinna: Involves the auricular cartilage after trauma or piercing; the ear itself is swollen, not the mastoid region.
• C. Malignant otitis externa: Occurs mainly in elderly diabetics/immunocompromised patients due to Pseudomonas; presents with severe otalgia and granulation tissue, not postauricular swelling in a child.
• D. Preauricular abscess: Swelling is anterior to the ear, not behind it.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with glaucoma is initiated on latanoprost ophthalmic solution 0.005%. Which of the following adverse effects of latanoprost should the patient be informed of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypertrichosis

Topical Latanoprost is likely to lead to hypertrichosis.

Adverse effects of Latanoprost include:

* Blurring of vision

* Conjunctival hyperaemia

* Eyelash thickening and darkening (hypertrichosis)

* Iris pigmentation

* Promotion of herpetic keratitis in a patient with a history of herpes infection if used preoperatively, cystoid macular edema following cataract surgery or in aphakic patients.

* Periorbital fat atrophy is seen as an adverse effect.

Latanoprost is a prostaglandin analogue and acts by increasing the uveoscleral outflow thus reducing the IOP. Latanoprost is preferred over β-blockers due to its decreased systemic side effects.

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a bilateral, symmetrical disease with an adult-onset type. In this condition, there is an increase in the IOP due to trabecular sclerosis leading to decreased aqueous outflow. The clinical features include headache, difficulty in dark adaptation, frequent change of glasses, and blurring of vision. On ocular examination, an open anterior chamber angle, glaucomatous optic nerve head changes, visual field defects, and an increased IOP of more than 21mmHg are noted.

Topical PGF2 alpha (prostaglandin) analogs are used as a first choice in the treatment of open-angle glaucoma. Latanoprost is the most commonly used. Travoprost and bimatoprost are the other drugs available.

Other options:

Option C: Cholinergic and anticholinesterase agents for topical ophthalmic use can have adverse effects of retinal detachment or iris cysts.

Option D: Beta-blockers such as timolol, though historically popular, are not ideal first-choice agents because they are contraindicated in patients with asthma, heart block, or bradycardia, and can cause systemic side effects like bronchospasm and bradycardia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient hailing from Delhi presents with fever, arthralgia, and extensive petechial rash for 3 days. Lab investigations revealed a hemoglobin of 9 g/dL, a white blood cell count of 9000 cells/mm3, a platelet count of 20000 cells/mm3, and a prolonged bleeding time. The clotting time was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dengue

The given clinical vignette is suggestive of dengue fever.

Dengue is an acute febrile disease caused by the mosquito-borne dengue viruses (DENVs), consisting of four serotypes (DENV 1 to 4), that are members of the Flaviviridae family, genus Flavivirus.

Dengue virus is transmitted from person to person by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

After an incubation period of 3–15 days, classical dengue fever begins with an abrupt onset of high fever. The condition is self-limiting though debilitating with headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, arthralgia, petechiae rash, and leucopenia. A macular-papular recovery rash appears 3–4 days after the onset of fever, and it usually starts on the trunk before spreading peripherally. The rash in dengue appears as 'white islands in a red sea' due to erythema with petechiae.

Shown below is an image of the rash in dengue:

Dengue fever is sometimes referred to as ‘break bone fever’ due to associated severe muscle and joint pain or ‘seven-day fever’ since the symptoms usually persist for 7 days.

The diseases range in severity from undifferentiated acute febrile illness, classical dengue fever (DF), to the life-threatening conditions dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF)/dengue shock syndrome (DSS).

DHF is associated with:

* plasma leakage and hemoconcentration

* hemorrhagic tendencies

* Increased vascular permeability

* Thrombocytopenia

DSS is distinguished from DHF by the presence of cardiovascular compromise, which occurs when plasma leakage into the interstitial spaces results in shock. DSS is a fatal condition. Common clinical warning signs for DSS include a rapidly increasing hematocrit, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and a narrowing or absence of blood pressure.

Other options:

Option B: Malaria is a protozoal disease caused by Plasmodium species. It is transmitted by the female anopheles mosquito. Here, the definitive host is the anopheles mosquito and humans are the intermediate hosts. Clinical features are periodic bouts of fever with chills and rigors, followed by anemia, splenomegaly, and hepatomegaly.

Option C: Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by trombiculid mites. The incubation period is 1-3 weeks. The patient typically develops a characteristic eschar which is a punched-out ulcer covered with a blackened scab at the site of the mite bite, with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. Here is a picture of the eschar.

Option D: Typhoid (enteric) fever is a systemic disease manifested by fever and abdominal pain caused by Salmonella typhi or Salmonella paratyphi.

Clinical features include fever, abdominal pain, headache, chills, myalgia, malaise, diarrhea, sweating, nausea, and vomiting. Rose spots are the classic cutaneous manifestation of typhoid fever, which presents as pink macules on the abdomen and the chest. Hepatosplenomegaly and relative bradycardia might be seen. The WBC count may be normal or low.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: High fat intake according to FDA is?
options: Diet should contain 400 kcal from carbohydrates
Diet should contain 800 kcal from fat
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diet should contain total 1000 kcal

High fat intake according to FDA is a diet that should contain a total of 1000 kcal.

High fat diets have low carbohydrates, <50 grams/day. This equates to <250 kcal/day in the form of carbohydrates, not 400 kcal (option A). The percentage of calories from fat is >50% (option D), which would equate to about 500-600 kcal from fats (option C). The diet should contain a total of 800 - 1000 kcal.

Ketogenic diets mainly incorporate low carbohydrates (<50 grams/day), low protein, and high fats. Gluconeogenesis from the glucogenic amino acids in the diet and fat oxidation are utilized to meet the metabolic demands of the body. Ketogenic diets are especially useful for the treatment of intractable epilepsy.
questions.learning: Diet should contain total 1000 kcal High fat intake according to FDA is a diet that should contain a total of 1000 kcal. High fat diets have low carbohydrates, 50% (option D), which would equate to about 500-600 kcal from fats (option C).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In an asymptomatic individual, what is the most appropriate diagnostic criterion for diabetes mellitus according to the ADA 2023 guidelines?
options: Oral glucose tolerance test: 2 hrs value
questions.explanation: According to the ADA 2023 guidelines, the diagnostic criteria for diabetes mellitus in an asymptomatic patient include: a Fasting Plasma Glucose (FPG) , an HbA1c , or a 2-hour plasma glucose during an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT). Therefore, Option A is the only correct diagnostic threshold listed. HbA1c of 5.9% (Option B) falls into the prediabetes range (5.7-6.4%). Fasting glucose (approx. ) (Option C) is completely normal. 2-hour glucose (approx. ) (Option D) is also within the normal or prediabetic range. For an asymptomatic patient, these tests usually require confirmation with a second test result from a different day. Accurate diagnosis is essential to begin early lifestyle and pharmacological interventions to prevent the progression of the disease and its subsequent systemic complications

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 2-year-old presents with excessive watery diarrhoea and severe dehydration. What is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rotavirus

The given clinical scenario with complaints of non-bloody diarrhoea and dehydration in a child suggests rotavirus.

Rotavirus is the most common identifiable viral cause of diarrhoea in children below the age of 5 years and is most frequent between 6-24 months of age. The incubation period is 1-3 days. Most cases are asymptomatic or with mild symptoms like watery diarrhoea, vomiting, low-grade fever, and temporary lactose intolerance. Diagnosis can be made by rapid antigen detection of rotavirus in stool specimens.

Treatment is supportive, including hydration and correction of fluid and electrolyte imbalance. The main goals of treatment are avoiding and treating dehydration. Maintaining nutrition is a secondary goal.

Other options:

Option A: Trichuris trichiura causes rectal prolapse in children (characteristic feature), chronic dysentery, anemia, poor growth, and developmental defects. The disease may result either due to the mechanical effect of the worms or an allergic reaction to the parasite.

Option B: Shigella causes Shigellosis, which is a spectrum of symptoms consisting of 4 phases:

1. Incubation

2. Watery diarrhoea: Fever, watery diarrhoea, anorexia

3. Dysentry: Bloody mucopurulent stools

4. Post-infectious complication: Hemolytic-uremic syndrome, reactive arthritis, and toxic megacolon.

Option D: Yersinia enterocolitica causes diarrhoea with symptoms resembling appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis). The patients present with abdominal pain, which can be localised to the right iliac fossa, thus mimicking appendicitis.

questions.text: A patient undergoes surgery for a pilonidal sinus. Which type of flap is typically used in this procedure?
questions.explanation: The image shows a curved, double-lobed flap closure, which is characteristic of a bilobed flap. This technique is commonly used in pilonidal sinus surgery (e.g., off-midline closure procedures) to redistribute tension and flatten the natal cleft, reducing recurrence. A bilobed flap consists of two adjacent flaps that are transposed sequentially to close a defect, allowing: 1. Tension-free closure 2. Better cosmetic outcome 3. Reduced risk of recurrence in pilonidal disease Why other options are incorrect: (A) Fasciocutaneous rotation flap: Involves a broad arc rotation, not the characteristic double-lobed design (C) Transposition flap: Single flap moved across defect; does not show the two-lobed pattern (D) Random pattern flap: Refers to blood supply type, not a specific flap design The distinct double-lobed appearance confirms this as a bilobed flap, commonly used in pilonidal sinus surgery

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the yoke muscle of the right lateral rectus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Left medial rectus

The right lateral rectus and left medial rectus represent a pair of yoke muscles.

Yoke muscles are also known as contralateral synergists. They are pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contracts simultaneously during version movements. Version movements also known as conjugate movements are synchronous (simultaneous) symmetric movements of both eyes in the same direction.

Examples:

* Right MR and Left LR

* Right LR and Left MR

* Right SO and Left IR

* Right IO and Left SR

* Right SR and Left IO

* Right IR and Left SO

(MR: Medial rectus; LR: Lateral rectus; SO: Superior oblique; IO: Inferior oblique; SR: Superior rectus; IR: Inferior rectus.)

These pairs of contralateral synergists receive equal and simultaneous innervation during version movements according to Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation.

Pearl PF1399: Laws governing ocular movements

Sherrington’s Law of Reciprocal Innervation

During ocular motility, an increased flow of innervation to the contracting muscle is accompanied by the decreased flow of innervation to the relaxing antagonist muscle.

Example:

During dextroversion, an increased innervation flow to the right lateral rectus (LR) and left medial rectus (MR) is accompanied by decreased flow to the right MR and left LR.

Herring’s Law of Equal Innervation

According to this law, equal and simultaneous innervation flows from the brain to the contralateral synergists and contralateral antagonists.

Example:

* During convergence: Both medial recti get equal innervation

* During dextroversion: Right LR and left MR get equal innervation

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman presents with a rapidly growing, painless mass in her right breast that she first noticed about 3 months ago. On physical examination, the mass is well-circumscribed, lobulated, and larger than 5 cm in diameter. A history of a similar lesion occurred 2 years back also. A core needle biopsy is performed, and the histological examination reveals the image as shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Phyllodes tumour

• Age: 42 years (phyllodes usually occurs in middle-aged women).
• Rapidly growing mass; Large size (>5 cm).
• Well-circumscribed and lobulated; History of recurrence.

Histopathology shows:

• Leaf-like (phyllodes) architecture with Cleft-like spaces
• Hypercellular stroma

Suggests phyllodes tumor > fibroadenoma.

| Fibroadenoma | Small, slow growing, common in young women

| Ductal papilloma | Usually causes nipple discharge

Double target sign is seen patients with CSF rhinorrhea. The nasal discharge in a patient with CSF rhinorrhea after head trauma is mixed with blood. When this discharge is collected on a filter paper, it shows a double target sign with a central red spot and a peripheral lighter halo.

Pearl PF1086: Features of CSF rhinorrhea

* Reservoir sign - In CSF rhinorrhea, the fluid which had collected in the sinuses, particularly sphenoid, empties into the nose.

* Double target sign or Halo sign or Target sign - CSF is mixed with blood and collected on a piece of filter paper. It shows a central red spot (blood) and a peripheral lighter halo.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: During a field visit, an epidemiologist observes mosquito larvae resting parallel to the water surface, without a siphon tube, and having palmate hairs on their abdominal segments. Based on these characteristics, which mosquito species do these larvae most likely belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Anopheles

Anopheles mosquito larvae characteristically rest parallel to the water surface due to the absence of a siphon tube.

They possess palmate hairs on abdominal segments, which help maintain this horizontal position.

In contrast, Aedes and Culex larvae have siphon tubes and hang at an angle, while Mansonia larvae attach to aquatic plants for respiration.
questions.learning: Anopheles Anopheles mosquito larvae characteristically rest parallel to the water surface due to the absence of a siphon tube. They possess palmate hairs on abdominal segments, which help maintain this horizontal position.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with recurrent renal calculi, proximal muscle weakness, and low mood. Laboratory evaluation shows elevated serum PTH with normal serum calcium. Primary hyperparathyroidism is suspected. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for preoperative localization of the abnormal gland?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tc-99m sestamibi scan

• Recurrent renal stones + proximal weakness + depression → classic hyperparathyroid symptom cluster
• ↑ PTH with normal Ca → early / normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism

Why Tc-99m Sestamibi is IOC

• Mechanism: Radiotracer (Tc-99m sestamibi) is taken up by mitochondria-rich parathyroid adenoma cells
• Shows persistent uptake in abnormal parathyroid tissue (vs thyroid washout)
• High sensitivity for detecting single adenoma (most common cause)

Step 4: Why not other options?

• A) Neck ultrasound

• Operator dependent
• Misses ectopic glands

• B) MRI neck

• Used only if sestamibi inconclusive

• D) CT neck

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 64-year-old male with a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea. He is compliant with his medications. An echocardiogram reveals normal systolic function and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction, left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, and a preserved ejection fraction (EF 60%). His BNP is elevated at 980 pg/mL. He has had two hospital admissions for heart failure in the past year. He is currently euvolemic and is on optimal doses of beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Perform coronary angiography to rule out ischemic cardiomyopathy
Initiate loop diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors
Start digoxin to enhance myocardial contractility
Initiate Ivabradine to reduce heart rate and improve diastolic filling
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate loop diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors

This patient has HFpEF (preserved EF, diastolic dysfunction, LVH, LA enlargement, elevated BNP). Management focuses on symptom control and reducing hospitalizations, not increasing contractility. Unlike HFrEF, HFpEF has limited mortality-reducing therapies. However two important treatments help:

1️⃣ Diuretics

Purpose:

• Reduce pulmonary congestion
• Control volume overload

Loop diuretics commonly used:

• Furosemide
• Torsemide

SGLT2 inhibitors improve outcomes and reduce HF admissions in HFpEF, while loop diuretics relieve congestion. They improve:

• Diuresis
• Cardiac metabolism
• Renal protection

| Feature | HFrEF | HFpEF

| ------- | ----- | -----

| EF | ↓ (<40%) | Normal (>50%)

| Problem | Weak contraction | Stiff ventricle

| Therapy | ACEi, BB, ARNI, MRA | Diuretics, SGLT2i

Digoxin and ivabradine have no proven outcome benefit in HFpEF, and ranolazine is for angina, not HF control.
questions.learning: Initiate loop diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors — This patient has HFpEF (preserved EF, diastolic dysfunction, LVH, LA enlargement, elevated BNP). Management focuses on symptom control and reducing hospitalizations, not increasing contractility.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea for 3 months and a history of untreated hypertension. Examination reveals bilateral basal crackles and dullness to percussion with decreased breath sounds over the right lung base. Chest X-ray shows a right-sided pleural effusion. The underlying mechanism is suspected to be cardiac dysfunction leading to fluid accumulation in the lungs and pleural space. Which of the following combinations of pleuropulmonary changes is most consistent with this condition?
options: Increased Vascular Permeability; Normal Hydrostatic Pressure; Normal Oncotic Pressure; Decreased Lymphatic Flow
Increased Vascular Permeability; Increased Hydrostatic Pressure; Decreased Oncotic Pressure; Decreased Lymphatic Flow
Normal Vascular Permeability; Normal Hydrostatic Pressure; Decreased Oncotic Pressure; Increased Lymphatic Flow
Normal Vascular Permeability; Increased Hydrostatic Pressure; Normal Oncotic Pressure; Increased Lymphatic Flow
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Normal Vascular Permeability; Increased Hydrostatic Pressure; Normal Oncotic Pressure; Increased Lymphatic Flow

Pleural effusion due to congestive heart failure (CHF) is a transudate caused by increased hydrostatic pressure, with normal vascular permeability and compensatory increase in lymphatic drainage.

• Hypertension → left ventricular dysfunction → ↑ pulmonary venous pressure
• Leads to:

• ↑ Hydrostatic pressure → fluid transudation
• Normal permeability (no inflammation)
• Normal oncotic pressure
• ↑ Lymphatic flow (compensatory)

Why Other Options are Incorrect:

• A & B → suggest inflammation/exudate (↑ permeability)
• C → decreased oncotic pressure (e.g., nephrotic syndrome)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy for the past 4 months. A lymph node biopsy image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma

Recognize Nodular Lymphocyte Predominant Hodgkin Lymphoma (NLPHL) by its characteristic histopathological finding of lymphocyte-predominant (LP or “popcorn”) cells within a background of small reactive B lymphocytes. Unlike classical Hodgkin lymphoma, NLPHL lacks classical Reed–Sternberg cells and has a distinct immunophenotype.

Why not the other options?

• A. Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL): Diffuse sheets of large atypical B cells without LP (“popcorn”) cells; aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
• C. Nodular Sclerosis Hodgkin Lymphoma: Characterized by lacunar Reed–Sternberg cells and broad collagen bands dividing the lymph node into nodules; most common subtype in young adults.
• D. Mixed Cellularity Hodgkin Lymphoma: Numerous classical Reed–Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory background (lymphocytes, eosinophils, plasma cells, histiocytes); commonly associated with EBV.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct statement regarding Huntington's chorea?
options: It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder
There is loss of function type of mutation
There are abnormal repeats of CUG
Abnormality is seen due to mutation in chromosome 6
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a trinucleotide repeat disorder

Huntington's chorea is a trinucleotide repeat disorder.

It is an autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder. It is caused by CAG trinucleotide repeats (>40). It occurs due to a gain-of-function (expansion) mutation in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4p.

The disease shows genetic anticipation and has an early-onset (2-3 decades) if inherited from the father.

Cognitive impairment is an early feature. Pathologically, atrophy of caudate and putamen with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly is seen. Decreased acetylcholine leads to dementia and decreased GABA and increased dopamine lead to chorea.

Treatment consists of haloperidol and tetrabenazine.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with occupational exposure to benzene presents with repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature. This occupational exposure will predispose him to which of the following cancers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leukemia

Occupational exposure to benzene predisposes to leukemia. The given clinical history of repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature with benzene exposure points towards a diagnosis of leukemia.

Benzene is oxidized to an epoxide through hepatic CYP2E1. The epoxide and other metabolites disrupt progenitor cell differentiation in the bone marrow and lead to marrow aplasia and acute myeloid leukemia.

Acute myeloid leukemia is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation. This leads to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. The replacement of the marrow with blasts produces marrow failure and complications related to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

Other options:

Option B: Exposure to arsenic and its compounds, asbestos, beryllium and its compounds, chromium compounds, nickel compounds, radon, and its decay products can cause lung cancer.

Option C: Exposure to aryl amines, particularly 2-naphthylamine and related compounds, cyclophosphamide, cigarette smoking, irradiation can cause bladder cancer.

Option D: Exposure to UV rays, arsenic, and its compounds can cause skin cancer.
questions.learning: Leukemia Occupational exposure to benzene predisposes to leukemia. The given clinical history of repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature with benzene exposure points towards a diagnosis of leukemia.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following undergoes Hofmann elimination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Atracurium

Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation.

Rocuronium, and vecuronium are dependent on the liver for excretion. Pancuronium excretion is primarily renal. A small percentage of the drug is excreted through bile (hepatic elimination).
questions.learning: Atracurium Atracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination, which is spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation. Rocuronium, and vecuronium are dependent on the liver for excretion.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is true about perimetry?
options: Kinetic perimetry is used in quantification and tracking of visual changes in established glaucoma
In Static perimetry, stimulus intensity is held constant and moved centrally with detection
Visual field defect to be classified as glaucoma, it should have the corresponding optic nerve head abnormalities
Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot

Early signs of glaucoma in perimetry include generalized constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot.

Progression of visual field changes seen in glaucoma:

Early non-specific changes

Isopter contraction

Baring of blind spot: Exclusion of blind spot from the central field

Early significant changes

Peripheral nasal step (may be early or late)

Paracentral scotoma in Bjerrum's area.

Siedel’s  scotoma: Paracentral scotoma joins the blind spot

Late significant changes

Arcuate or Bjerrum scotoma

Ring or Double arcuate scotoma: When 2 arcuate scotomas join together

Roenne’s central nasal step

Advanced glaucomatous field defects

Tubular vision

No light perception: Complete visual field defect.

Perimetry is the procedure of estimating the extent of the visual fields. There are 2 types of perimetry - kinetic and static. In kinetic perimetry, a target of given luminance is moved from a non-seeing area in the periphery towards the center where it is perceived. In the static method, the location of a stimulus remains fixed, with the intensity increased until it is seen by the subject (threshold is reached) or decreased until it is no longer detected.

Charting of the visual fields is useful in the diagnosis of many disease conditions such as glaucoma, neurological disorders, and retinal diseases (e.g. retinitis pigmentosa) as well as following laser treatment of diabetic retinopathy.

Other options-

Option A: Static perimetry (not kinetic perimetry) is used in the quantification and tracking of visual changes in established glaucoma.

Option B: In Kinetic perimetry (not static perimetry), stimulus intensity is held constant and moved centrally with detection.

Option C: Optic disc changes are much greater than visual field changes. Therefore, visual field defects need not correspond to optic nerve head abnormalities to be classified as glaucoma.
questions.learning: Early signs include generalised constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot Early signs of glaucoma in perimetry include generalized constriction of isopters and baring of blind spot.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department following a fire incident. Her face and lower limbs are spared. Based on this distribution, calculate the total percentage of body surface area burned.
questions.explanation: Using the "Wallace Rule of Nines" for an adult, we calculate the total body surface area (TBSA) by identifying the affected regions. In this case: the anterior torso (chest and abdomen) accounts for 18%, the posterior torso (back) accounts for 18%, both arms (9% each) account for 18%, and the perineum accounts for 1%. Since the face (9%) and lower limbs (18% each) are spared, they are excluded. Summing the affected areas: . Option D (40–50%) is the closest range that fits this calculation, as minor variations in arm involvement or patches of spared skin could reduce the total slightly. Options A, B, and C significantly underestimate the TBSA of a trunk-and-arm burn. Accurate TBSA calculation is vital for guiding fluid resuscitation using formulas like the Parkland formula

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presented to the OPD with an abnormal gait. On examination, when the patient was asked to stand on the left foot, a right-sided hip drop was observed. Which of the following muscles are paralyzed in this patient?
options: Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus

The examination of the patient indicates a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait), with sagging on the right side. It is seen in paralysis of the left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles which are supplied by the left superior gluteal nerve.

The superior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus.

Mechanism of actions of gluteus medius and minimus:

* When the leg on one side is lifted off the ground, the gluteus medius and minimus muscles, on the opposite supported side, exert traction on the hip bone by acting from the femur. This action results in the slight raising of the pelvis on the unsupported side, which helps maintain the trunk in the upright position.

* When the gluteus medius and minimus are paralyzed, the pelvis sinks down on the unsupported (normal) side, when the patient tries to stand on the affected limb.

Inferior gluteal nerve supplies the gluteus maximus muscle.

The below GIF shows a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait) with a left superior gluteal nerve injury.

In the GIF, when the person lifts up his right leg and tries to stand on the left leg, the right pelvis tilts down. This shows that the left side abduction mechanism is paralyzed and the right side is normal. The left superior gluteal nerve is injured in this case since it supplies the left gluteus medius and minimus.

Note: These patients can also have a characteristic lurching gait.
questions.learning: Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus — The examination of the patient indicates a positive Trendelenburg's sign (Trendelenburg's gait), with sagging on the right side.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Kraissl’s lines are
options: Point of maximum tension in a fracture
Collagen and elastin lines in stab injury
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Relaxed Tension lines in skin

Kraissl's lines are relaxed tension lines in the skin. They lie perpendicular to the long axis of the underlying muscle. They were described in living individuals and reflect underlying muscle action.

Image of Kraissl's lines:

Langer's lines correspond to the natural orientation of collagen fibers in the dermis and are generally parallel to the orientation of the underlying muscle fibers. They were described in cadavers in reference to rigor mortis.

Image of Langer's lines:

Borge's lines are also relaxed skin tension lines observed by pinching the skin in living individuals.

Borge's lines and Kraissl's lines are a better guide for elective incisions in the face and body than Langer's lines.

Linear incisions in the skin tend to have variable degrees of gaping. When a circular skin incision is performed, the skin defect acquires an elliptical configuration. By aligning circular incisions perpendicular to the muscle action, surgeons can minimize tension on the wound edges, reduce the risk of scar contracture, and achieve better cosmetic results.

Difference between Kraissl's line and Langer's line

Kraissl's line
Langer's line

Described in living individuals
Described in cadavers

Lie perpendicular to the long axis of the underlying muscle
Correspond to the natural orientation of collagen fibers

Reflects the action of the underlying muscle
They are skin tension vectors observed in the stretched skin of cadavers exhibiting rigor mortis
